name: Numbers
sourceNote: Written freshly, thought for thought, from the oldest Hebrew, Greek, and Aramaic witnesses (the Masoretic Text with the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, and the Samaritan Pentateuch). © 2026 Jose Santiago. All rights reserved.

verses.text: In the Wilderness of Sinai,{a} inside the meeting tent, Yahweh spoke to Moses. It was the first day of the second month (April-May),{b} in the second year since Israel left Egypt. He said,
“Take a census{c} of all Israel’s people. Write down every man’s name, sorted by clan and by family.
You and Aaron are to list every man in Israel who is twenty or older and able to fight, unit by unit.{d}
One man from each tribe will help you, each the head of his own family.
“These are the men who will stand with you. For Reuben, Elizur{e} (Shedeur’s son).
For Simeon, Shelumiel (Zurishaddai’s son).{f}
For Judah, Nahshon (Amminadab’s son).
For Issachar, Nethanel (Zuar’s son).
For Zebulun, Eliab (Helon’s son).
For Joseph’s two tribes: Elishama (Ammihud’s son) for Ephraim, and Gamaliel (Pedahzur’s son) for Manasseh.
For Benjamin, Abidan (Gideoni’s son).
For Dan, Ahiezer (Ammishaddai’s son).
For Asher, Pagiel (Ochran’s son).
For Gad, Eliasaph (Deuel’s son).{g}
For Naphtali, Ahira (Enan’s son).”
These were the ones picked from the assembly, the heads of their ancestral tribes and the chiefs of Israel’s units.{h}
Moses and Aaron took these men, each one named,
and on the first day of the second month (April-May) they called the whole community together. Each man twenty or older was registered by his clan and his family, one by one,
just as Yahweh had ordered Moses. So he counted them in the Wilderness of Sinai.
First came Reuben, the oldest son of Israel. His descendants were recorded by clan and family, with every man of twenty or more who could serve in the army listed by name:
Reuben’s tribe came to 46,500 men.
Next came Simeon. His descendants were recorded by clan and family, with every man of twenty or more who could serve in the army listed by name:
Simeon’s tribe came to 59,300 men.
Next, Gad. Its men of twenty and over who were fit for the army were written down by clan and family:
Gad’s tribe came to 45,650 men.
Next, Judah. Its men of twenty and over who were fit for the army were written down by clan and family:
Judah’s tribe came to 74,600 men.
Next, Issachar. Its men of twenty and over who were fit for the army were written down by clan and family:
Issachar’s tribe came to 54,400 men.
Next, Zebulun. Its men of twenty and over who were fit for the army were written down by clan and family:
Zebulun’s tribe came to 57,400 men.
Then came the descendants of Joseph. First, Ephraim: all its men of twenty and over who could go to war were listed by clan and family:
Ephraim’s tribe came to 40,500 men.
Manasseh followed. Its men of twenty and over who could go to war were listed by clan and family:
Manasseh’s tribe came to 32,200 men.
Then Benjamin. Its men of twenty and over who could go to war were listed by clan and family:
Benjamin’s tribe came to 35,400 men.
Then Dan. Its men of twenty and over who could go to war were listed by clan and family:
Dan’s tribe came to 62,700 men.
Asher came next. Its men of twenty and over who could go to war were listed by clan and family:
Asher’s tribe came to 41,500 men.
Last was Naphtali. Its men of twenty and over who could go to war were listed by clan and family:
Naphtali’s tribe came to 53,400 men.
Moses and Aaron did this counting together with the twelve leaders of Israel, one man for each family.
The total of all the Israelite men twenty or older who could serve in the army, counted by family,
in all came to 603,550.{i}
Levi’s tribe, though, was left out of this count.
This was because Yahweh had said to Moses,
“Leave Levi’s tribe out. Do not include them when you take the census of Israel.

Rather, give the Levites charge of the dwelling that holds the covenant, along with all its furnishings and everything that goes with it. They will carry the dwelling and its furnishings, tend to it, and set up camp around it.
When the dwelling is to move, the Levites take it down. When it is to be set up, the Levites put it up. Any outsider{j} who comes near must be put to death.
The other Israelites camp by units, each person in his own camp beside his own banner.

But the Levites set up camp right around the dwelling that holds the covenant, to keep my anger from striking the people of Israel. Guarding the dwelling that holds the covenant is the Levites’ duty.”
The Israelites carried out everything Yahweh had ordered Moses.

notes.text: Hebrew midbar, “wilderness,” open grazing land or steppe as well as desert. The book’s Hebrew title is Bemidbar, “In the Wilderness,” from this verse. The English title “Numbers” comes from the Greek (Arithmoi) and Latin (Numeri) titles, named for the two censuses in chapters 1 and 26.

Hebrew “on the first of the second month,” counting from the spring new year (Exodus 12:2). The second month, later called Iyyar (Ziv in 1 Kings 6:1), fell in April-May. The Hebrew months followed the moon, so each overlaps two of ours. This was one month after the tabernacle was set up (Exodus 40:17).
Hebrew “lift up the head,” an idiom for counting.
Or “by their armies.” Hebrew tsava, used of organized groups, especially for war.
Many names in this list contain a name for God: El (“God”), Shaddai (see the note at Exodus 6:3), or Tsur (“Rock”). Elizur means “my God is a rock.”
Shelumiel means “God is my peace.” Zurishaddai means “Shaddai is my rock.”
Most Hebrew copies read “Deuel” here and in 7:42, 47 and 10:20, but “Reuel” in 2:14. The letters d and r look much alike in Hebrew writing. The Greek Old Testament reads Ragouel every time.
Or “clans” or “units.” See the note at verse 46.

The census figures in this chapter and in chapter 26 add up exactly, and they are given here as the Hebrew has them. A total of 603,550 fighting men would mean a population of perhaps two million or more. The Hebrew word elef, usually “thousand,” can also mean a clan or a military unit (see verse 16; Judges 6:15; 1 Samuel 10:19). Some scholars have therefore suggested that the figures first counted units and men (for example, “46 units, 500 men”). Others hold that the numbers are literal, or that they are deliberately large symbolic figures. The same total appears in Exodus 38:26, and a similar one in Exodus 12:37. This translation keeps the numbers as written.
Hebrew zar, someone who is not a Levite.

verses.text: Yahweh addressed Moses and Aaron:
“Each Israelite is to camp under his own banner, near the emblems{a} of his family. They are to camp around the meeting tent, facing it from all sides at some distance.
“Judah’s camp, with its banner, takes the east side, where the sun rises, with its units. Judah’s leader is Nahshon son of Amminadab,
and his unit numbers 74,600.
Next to him camps the tribe of Issachar. Its leader is Nethanel son of Zuar,
and his unit numbers 54,400.
Then comes the tribe of Zebulun. Its leader is Eliab son of Helon,
and his unit numbers 57,400.
In all, Judah’s camp has 186,400 men in its units. They are first to march.
“Reuben’s camp, with its banner, takes the south side, with its units. Reuben’s leader is Elizur son of Shedeur,
and his unit numbers 46,500.
Next to him camps the tribe of Simeon. Its leader is Shelumiel son of Zurishaddai,
and his unit numbers 59,300.
Then comes the tribe of Gad. Its leader is Eliasaph son of Reuel,{b}
and his unit numbers 45,650.
In all, Reuben’s camp has 151,450 men in its units. They march second.
“After them the meeting tent moves out, with the Levites’ camp in the middle of the others. They march in the same order in which they camp, each in his own place under his own banner.
“Ephraim’s camp, with its banner, takes the west side, with its units. Ephraim’s leader is Elishama son of Ammihud,
and his unit numbers 40,500.
Next to him camps the tribe of Manasseh. Its leader is Gamaliel son of Pedahzur,
and his unit numbers 32,200.
Then comes the tribe of Benjamin. Its leader is Abidan son of Gideoni,
and his unit numbers 35,400.
In all, Ephraim’s camp has 108,100 men in its units. They march third.
“Dan’s camp, with its banner, takes the north side, with its units. Dan’s leader is Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai,
and his unit numbers 62,700.
Next to him camps the tribe of Asher. Its leader is Pagiel son of Ochran,
and his unit numbers 41,500.
Then comes the tribe of Naphtali. Its leader is Ahira son of Enan,
and his unit numbers 53,400.
In all, Dan’s camp has 157,600 men. They march last, each under his banner.”
These were the Israelites counted by family. The total for all the camps, by units, was 603,550.
The Levites were not counted with the other Israelites, as Yahweh had ordered Moses.
The Israelites did everything Yahweh ordered Moses. They camped under their banners, and they marched out the same way, each person with his own clan and family.

notes.text: Or “signs,” perhaps flags or standards. Hebrew degel (“banner”) marks each group of three tribes, and ot (“sign”) each family.
Hebrew Reuel. Elsewhere in Numbers most copies read Deuel. See the note at 1:14.

verses.text: This is the account of Aaron’s family and Moses’, beginning from when Yahweh spoke with Moses at Mount Sinai.
Aaron’s sons, in birth order: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
Those were Aaron’s sons, the priests who received anointing and were installed{a} to serve as priests.

Nadab and Abihu fell dead in front of Yahweh when they offered fire he had not approved, there in the Wilderness of Sinai. They left no sons,{b} so Eleazar and Ithamar took up the priests’ work in Aaron’s lifetime.
Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Have the tribe of Levi come forward and stand before Aaron the priest as his helpers.
They will take on duties for him and for the entire community at the front of the meeting tent, carrying out the labor of the dwelling.
They will be responsible for every piece of equipment in the meeting tent, and they will meet the Israelites’ obligations by working at the dwelling.
The Levites are to be handed over to Aaron and his sons as a gift, entirely his.{c}
Put Aaron and his sons in charge, and they will hold the priesthood. Any outsider who comes near must be put to death.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“I have myself taken the Levites from the Israelites to take the place of every firstborn child, the first to be born in each Israelite family. The Levites belong to me,
All firstborn are mine. On the day I killed Egypt’s firstborn, I claimed for myself every firstborn in Israel, whether person or animal. They are mine. I am Yahweh.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses in the Wilderness of Sinai and said,
“Take a count of Levi’s descendants by their families and clans, including every boy and man from the age of one month.”
So Moses counted them as Yahweh ordered, following his word.{d}
These were Levi’s sons, listed by name: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
Gershon’s clans came from his sons Libni and Shimei.
Kohath’s clans came from his sons Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel.
Merari’s clans came from his sons Mahli and Mushi. These were the Levite clans, listed by family.
The Libnites and Shimeites belonged to Gershon, and together they were the Gershonite clans.
Counting every male one month old or older, they numbered 7,500.
Behind the dwelling, to the west, was the Gershonites’ campsite.
Eliasaph son of Lael was the head of the Gershonite family.
In the meeting tent, the Gershonites cared for the dwelling, the tent with its covering, and the curtain at the tent’s entrance,
the hangings of the courtyard, the curtain at the courtyard entrance around the dwelling and the altar, and the ropes. They did all the work these needed.
The Amramites, Izharites, Hebronites, and Uzzielites belonged to Kohath. Together they were the Kohathite clans.
Counting every male one month old or older, they numbered 8,600.{e} They had charge of the holy place.
South of the dwelling was where the Kohathite clans pitched their tents.
Elizaphan son of Uzziel was the head of the Kohathite clans.
They cared for the chest, the table, the lampstand, the altars, the holy-place utensils used in service, and the screen, with all the work these involved.
Eleazar son of Aaron the priest was over all the Levite chiefs. He supervised the men who guarded the holy place.
The Mahlites and Mushites belonged to Merari, and together they made up the Merarite clans.
Counting every male one month old or older, they numbered 6,200.
The head of the Merarite family was Zuriel son of Abihail. North of the dwelling was their campsite.
The Merarites were responsible for the dwelling’s frames, crossbars, posts, bases, and all its equipment, together with the work these involved,
and for the posts around the courtyard with their bases, pegs, and ropes.

East of the dwelling, in front of the meeting tent where the sun came up, were the tents of Moses, Aaron, and Aaron’s sons. They guarded the holy place for the Israelites’ sake. Anyone not authorized who got close would be killed.
Moses and Aaron{f} counted the Levites by clan on Yahweh’s order, and every male from a month old up totaled 22,000.{g}
Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Count each firstborn Israelite male from the age of one month, and record how many names there are.
The Levites are mine to take in place of every Israelite firstborn, and the Levites’ animals in place of every firstborn animal belonging to the Israelites. I am Yahweh.”
So Moses counted all the firstborn Israelites, as Yahweh ordered him.
The firstborn males one month old or older, listed by name, numbered 22,273.
Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Accept the Levites in exchange for all Israel’s firstborn, and the Levites’ animals in exchange for Israel’s animals. The Levites belong to me. I am Yahweh.
For the 273 firstborn Israelites beyond the number of the Levites, a ransom price is due.
Collect about 2 ounces of silver{h} for each one, counted person by person, weighed by the standard of the holy place.
Hand it over to Aaron and his sons as payment for those extra people.”
So Moses collected the ransom money from those beyond the number bought back by the Levites.
From the firstborn of the Israelites he collected about 34 pounds of silver,{i} weighed by the standard of the holy place.
Following Yahweh’s word, as Yahweh had commanded him, Moses delivered the ransom money to Aaron and his sons.

notes.text: Hebrew “whose hand he filled,” the phrase for installing priests (Exodus 28:41).
See Leviticus 10:1-2.
Hebrew “given, given,” stressing that they are given completely. The Greek Old Testament and some other ancient copies read “given to me.” Compare 8:16.
Hebrew “mouth.”

So the Hebrew and the Greek Old Testament. Some scholars suggest “8,300,” which would make the three Levite clans add up to the 22,000 of verse 39 (7,500 + 8,300 + 6,200). In Hebrew, “six” (shesh) and “three” (shalosh) differ by only one letter.
In the Hebrew text the words “and Aaron” have dots above the letters, a sign that ancient scribes doubted they belonged. Some ancient copies leave them out.
The clan figures in verses 22, 28, and 34 add up to 22,300. See the note at verse 28.

Hebrew “five shekels,” about 2 ounces (57 grams). A shekel was about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams), though standards varied. The text adds, “the shekel is twenty gerahs.” A gerah was one twentieth of a shekel. On the “sanctuary shekel,” see Exodus 30:13.
Hebrew “1,365 shekels,” about 34 pounds (15.7 kilograms).

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron and said,
“Count the Kohath branch of the Levites, by clan and by family,
every man from thirty to fifty years old who comes to join the work crew{a} in the meeting tent.
The Kohathites’ work in the meeting tent concerns the most holy things.
“When the camp is about to move, Aaron and his sons go in, take down the curtain that screens the chest, and cover the covenant chest with it.
Over that they put a covering of fine leather,{b} then spread a solid blue cloth on top and put the carrying poles in place.
Over the table of the Presence they spread a blue cloth and set out the plates, spoons, bowls, and pitchers for drink offerings. The standing bread rests on the table as well.
Over all of it goes a scarlet cloth, then a layer of fine leather. Then the poles are slid in.
With a blue cloth they wrap the lampstand that gives light, along with its lamps, wick trimmers, trays, and every jar of oil used for it.
They wrap it and all its tools in a covering of fine leather and set it on a carrying frame.
Over the gold altar they spread a blue cloth, cover that with fine leather, and put its poles in place.
They gather all the tools used for service in the holy place, wrap them in blue cloth, cover them with fine leather, and set them on the carrying frame.
They clear the ashes from the altar, then cover it with a purple cloth.
They then arrange on it every tool used at the altar: fire pans, meat forks, shovels, and basins. Fine leather goes over it, and its poles are slid in.{c}

When Aaron and his sons have finished covering the holy place and all its objects, and the camp is ready to travel, the Kohathites come to do the carrying. But they may not touch the holy objects at all, or they will die. These are the things the Kohathites carry from the meeting tent.

“Eleazar, Aaron the priest’s son, has charge of the lamp oil, the sweet-smelling incense, the regular grain offering, and the anointing oil. He supervises the entire dwelling, with all its contents, and the holy place with its furnishings.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron and said,
“Make sure the Kohathite clans are not destroyed and lost from among the Levites.
To keep them alive and not let them die when they come near the most holy things, Aaron and his sons must go in first and assign each man his task and his load.
The Kohathites may not enter even for a moment{d} to see the holy things, or they will die.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Count the Gershon branch too, by family and by clan.
Count every man aged thirty to fifty who comes to serve in the work at the meeting tent.
Here is what the Gershonite clans do, both serving and carrying:
they carry the tent curtains of the dwelling and the meeting tent, its cover, the fine leather covering above it, the screen at the meeting tent’s entrance,

the courtyard hangings, the curtain at the courtyard gate that surrounds the dwelling and the altar, their ropes, and all the tools used for their work. They are to do all that needs doing with these.
All the Gershonites’ work, everything they carry and everything they do, takes place under the direction{e} of Aaron and his sons. Give them a list of the loads they are responsible for.
That is the work of the Gershonite clans at the meeting tent. Ithamar, the son of Aaron the priest, supervises{f} their duties.
“Count the Merari branch too, by clan and by family.
Count every man from thirty up to fifty who enters to take part in the labor at the meeting tent.
Their loads, as their share of the meeting tent’s work, are the dwelling’s frames, crossbars, posts, and bases,
plus the posts around the courtyard with their bases, pegs, and ropes, with all their equipment and tasks. Name the specific items each man is responsible to carry.
That is what the Merarite clans do, all their labor at the meeting tent, directed by Ithamar, Aaron the priest’s son.”
Moses, Aaron, and the community’s leaders counted the Kohathite clans by clan and by family,
every man from thirty to fifty years old who came to join the work in the meeting tent.
The count by clan was 2,750.
This was the total for the Kohathite clans, all who served in the meeting tent. Moses and Aaron counted them by Yahweh’s word given through Moses.
The Gershon branch was counted by clan and by family,
every man from thirty to fifty years old who came to join the work in the meeting tent.
The count by clan and family was 2,630.
This was the total for the Gershonite clans, all who served in the meeting tent. Moses and Aaron counted them at Yahweh’s word.
The Merari branch was counted by clan and by family,
every man from thirty to fifty years old who came to join the work in the meeting tent.
The count by clan was 3,200.
This was the total for the Merarite clans, whom Moses and Aaron counted at Yahweh’s word given through Moses.
The grand total of the Levites counted by Moses, Aaron, and Israel’s leaders, by clan and by family,
every man from thirty to fifty years old who came to do the work of serving and carrying in the meeting tent,
came to 8,580.
Yahweh spoke through Moses, and each man was given his own job and load. So they were counted by Moses, just as Yahweh had ordered.

notes.text: Hebrew tsava, “host,” here the organized work crew of the Levites. In 8:24 the starting age is twenty-five. Compare 1 Chronicles 23:24-27, where it is twenty.
Hebrew tahash. See the note at Exodus 25:5. The same word is used in verses 8-14 and 25.

The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Greek Old Testament add, “They are to take a purple cloth and cover the basin and its stand, put it in a covering of fine leather, and put it on the carrying frame.” This is one of the longer readings that the Samaritan Pentateuch shares with other ancient copies in Numbers. See the note at 10:10.
Hebrew “as a swallowing,” perhaps “even for the time it takes to swallow.”
Hebrew “mouth.”
Hebrew “hand.” The same word is used in verse 33.

verses.text: Yahweh told Moses,
“Order the Israelites to send away from the camp anyone with a skin disease{a} that makes a person unclean, anyone with a bodily discharge, and anyone made unclean by touching a dead body.
Men and women alike must go outside the camp. Do not let them make the camp unclean, since I live among you.”
The Israelites obeyed and sent these people outside the camp. They did just what Yahweh had told Moses.
Yahweh also told Moses,
“Tell the Israelites: Suppose a man or woman does wrong to someone else and so is unfaithful to Yahweh. When that person realizes the guilt,
he must admit what he did. He must pay back the full value of what he took, add one fifth more, and hand it to the person he wronged.

If that person has died and has no close relative{b} to receive the payment, the payment belongs to Yahweh and goes to the priest. The ram of atonement, which makes things right for the guilty person, is separate from this.
Every contribution that Israelites set apart and bring to a priest belongs to that priest.
What people dedicate stays theirs until they give it, and then it is the priest’s.”
Yahweh told Moses,
“Speak to the Israelites and say: Suppose a man’s wife strays and betrays him.
Another man sleeps with her, but her husband never learns of it. She is unclean, yet there is no witness and nobody caught her.
Then a feeling of jealousy comes over her husband, and he suspects her, whether she really made herself unclean or not.

He must take his wife to the priest and bring an offering for her: about 2 quarts of barley flour.{c} He must not pour oil on it or add frankincense, because it is a grain offering about jealousy, one that calls guilt to mind.
“The priest will bring her forward and have her stand in front of Yahweh.
He will fill a clay jar with holy water, take some dust from the floor of the dwelling, and stir it into the water.
With the woman standing before Yahweh, the priest will uncover her hair and place the grain offering of jealousy in her hands. He himself will hold the bitter water that brings a curse.

Next the priest has her swear an oath. He tells her, ‘If no man has had relations with you, and you have never strayed into impurity while under your husband’s roof, the bitter water that brings a curse will not harm you.
But if you have strayed while married, and made yourself unclean by relations with someone besides your husband,’
(then the priest puts the woman under the oath of the curse) ‘may Yahweh turn you into a curse and a warning among your people, by making your thigh shrink and your belly swell.{d}
May this cursed water enter your body, swelling your belly and shrinking your thigh.’ The woman must answer, ‘Amen. Amen.’{e}
“The priest will then write out these curses on a scroll and wash the writing off into the water of bitterness.
He will make the woman drink the bitter, cursing water, and it will enter her and turn bitter.
He will take the grain offering of jealousy from her hand, lift it up in front of Yahweh, and bring it to the altar.
Then he will scoop out a handful of the grain as the part that stands for the whole, burn it on the altar, and after that have the woman drink the water.

Once she has drunk it, if she has made herself unclean and betrayed her husband, the cursing water will enter her and turn bitter. Her belly will swell, her thigh will shrink, and her people will use her name as a curse.
But if the woman is innocent and has not made herself unclean, she will be cleared and can still bear children.
“This is the law for jealousy, for a wife who strays and makes herself unclean while married,
or for a husband who is overcome by a jealous feeling toward his wife. The priest will have the woman stand before Yahweh and carry out this whole law.
The husband is cleared of any guilt, but the woman bears her own.”

notes.text: Hebrew tsara’at, a word for various skin diseases (Leviticus 13-14), traditionally translated “leprosy” but not limited to what is now called leprosy (Hansen’s disease).
Hebrew go’el, the nearest relative, who had the right and duty to receive or pay redemption on behalf of a family member.
Hebrew “a tenth of an ephah of barley flour,” about 2.2 liters. An ephah was about three-fifths of a bushel (22 liters); standards varied.
The exact meaning of “thigh” (perhaps a euphemism for the reproductive organs) and of the physical effects is uncertain. They may describe a miscarriage or infertility (compare verse 28).
Hebrew amen, “so be it,” a word of solemn agreement.

subheads.11: The test for a jealous husband

verses.text: Yahweh told Moses,
“Tell the Israelites: When a man or woman takes the special vow of a Nazirite,{a} setting themselves apart for Yahweh,
that person must stay away from wine and other strong drink. No vinegar made from wine or strong drink, no grape juice, and no grapes, fresh or dried.
For the whole time of the vow, nothing that comes from the grapevine may be eaten, not even the seeds or skins.{b}
“For the whole time of the vow, no razor may touch the head. Until the days of the vow are over, the person is holy and must let the hair grow long.
“For the whole time of the vow to Yahweh, a Nazirite must not go near a dead body.
Not even if a father, mother, brother, or sister dies may a Nazirite become unclean, because the sign of devotion to God is on the head.
Throughout the vow, the person is holy to Yahweh.

“Suppose someone suddenly collapses and dies next to a Nazirite, and the hair that was set apart becomes unclean. Then the Nazirite must shave his head on the day of cleansing, which is the seventh day.
On day eight he brings a pair of doves, or a pair of young pigeons, to the priest at the meeting tent’s entrance.
One bird the priest offers as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering, making things right for him after he sinned by being near a corpse. That same day he sets his head apart again.
He starts his time of vow over again for Yahweh and brings a year-old male lamb as a guilt offering. The earlier days do not count,{c} since the vow was made unclean.
“This is the law for a Nazirite when the time of the vow is over. He is brought to the entrance of the meeting tent

He presents Yahweh with these gifts: for a burnt offering, a male lamb one year old and perfect; for a sin offering, a one-year-old female lamb, also perfect; and for a peace offering, one perfect ram.
With these goes a basket of bread without yeast, loaves of fine flour mixed with oil and thin breads without yeast spread with oil, and also their grain offerings and drink offerings.
The priest will bring these in front of Yahweh and present the sin offering and the burnt offering.
He will offer the ram to Yahweh as a peace offering along with the basket of bread without yeast, as well as the grain offering and drink offering that go with it.
At the entrance of the meeting tent the Nazirite will shave off the hair he set apart, and put it into the fire under the peace offering.

After the Nazirite has shaved his head, the priest will take the boiled shoulder of the ram, one loaf without yeast from the basket, and one thin bread without yeast, and place them in the Nazirite’s hands.
He lifts these before Yahweh as a wave offering. They are holy and go to the priest, in addition to the lifted breast and the thigh that was contributed. Then the Nazirite is free to drink wine.
“That is the law for a Nazirite who vows an offering to Yahweh for the sake of the vow, plus anything more he can afford. He must do what he promised in his vow, following the law of a Nazirite.”
Yahweh told Moses,
“Say to Aaron and his sons, ‘Here is how you should bless the Israelites. Tell them:{d}
“Yahweh bless you and guard you.
Yahweh let his face shine upon you and treat you kindly.
Yahweh look kindly on you and give you peace.”’{e}
That is how they will put my name on the Israelites, and I will bless them.”

notes.text: Hebrew nazir, from nazar, “to separate” or “to dedicate.” Compare Samson (Judges 13:5), Samuel (1 Samuel 1:11), and Acts 18:18; 21:23-26.
The meaning of the two Hebrew words hartsannim and zag is uncertain; they may refer to unripe grapes and grape skins, or to seeds and skins.
Hebrew “will fall.”

The blessing in verses 24-26 has three lines of growing length, each naming Yahweh. A form of it is written on two small silver scrolls found at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem, dated to around 600 BC, among the oldest known texts of any biblical passage.
Hebrew shalom, wholeness and well-being, not merely the absence of conflict.

verses.text: Moses finished erecting the dwelling and anointed it, setting it and all its furnishings apart. He anointed and set apart the altar with all its equipment too.
Then the leaders of Israel, the heads of the ancestral families, made gifts. These were the tribal leaders, the ones who had overseen the census.
Their gift to Yahweh was six covered carts{a} along with twelve oxen. Two leaders shared a cart, and each leader gave an ox. They brought it all to the front of the dwelling.
Yahweh spoke to Moses:
“Receive these gifts from them. They will serve in the meeting tent’s work. Hand them over to the Levites, giving each man what his duties call for.”
Moses accepted the carts and oxen and handed them over to the Levites.
Two carts and four oxen went to the Gershonites, as their work called for.
To the Merarites he gave four carts and eight oxen, to suit their work, and Ithamar son of Aaron the priest oversaw them.
He gave none to the Kohathites, because their work was with the holy things, which they carried on their shoulders.
The leaders brought gifts for the altar’s dedication{b} on the day it was anointed. They set their gifts in front of the altar.
Yahweh told Moses, “Let one leader each day bring his gift for the dedication of the altar.”
Judah’s leader, Nahshon son of Amminadab, brought the first gift, on the opening day.

He brought one silver plate weighing about 3¼ pounds and one silver bowl weighing about 1¾ pounds, measured by the sanctuary standard. Each was filled with fine flour mixed with oil as a grain offering.{c}
He also gave a gold dish of about 4 ounces, filled with incense.{d}
He gave a ram, a young bull, and a lamb, male and one year old, to be burned whole.
For the sin offering there was a male goat.
He finished with a peace offering. It held two oxen, five rams, five billy goats, and five lambs, all male and each a year old. Nahshon son of Amminadab had given it.
Day two: Nethanel son of Zuar, who led Issachar’s tribe, stepped up with his gift.
His gift included a silver plate of about 3¼ pounds and a silver bowl of about 1¾ pounds, both weighed by the sanctuary standard, and both filled with oil-mixed fine flour for a grain offering.
There was a gold dish, about 4 ounces in weight, full of incense.
His burnt offering: one young bull, one ram, and one year-old lamb, a male.
A male goat served as his sin offering.
The peace offering that Nethanel son of Zuar brought was made up of two oxen, five rams, five billy goats, and five yearling male lambs.
Zebulun’s turn came on the third day, and its leader Eliab son of Helon presented what he had brought.
The silver he gave was a plate of about 3¼ pounds and a bowl of about 1¾ pounds, by the sanctuary’s weights. Fine flour mixed with oil filled both, to serve as a grain offering.
He added one gold dish weighing about 4 ounces, and it held incense.
To be burned whole, he supplied one male lamb a year old, one ram, and one young bull.
He added a billy goat as a sin offering.
His peace offering was two oxen, with five rams, five billy goats, and five male lambs a year old. Eliab son of Helon presented all of it.
On the fourth day, Reuben’s leader Elizur son of Shedeur came forward to give his gift.
He presented a silver plate (about 3¼ pounds) and a silver bowl (about 1¾ pounds) by the sanctuary standard, each one full of fine flour and oil blended for a grain offering.
A gold dish of about 4 ounces, packed with incense, came as well.
A young bull, a ram, and a male lamb in its first year were his burnt offering.
He gave a male goat for the sin offering.
Peace offering: five rams, five billy goats, five yearling male lambs, and two oxen. That was what Elizur son of Shedeur offered.
The fifth day’s gift came from Shelumiel son of Zurishaddai, who commanded the tribe of Simeon.

Two silver pieces came with him: a plate that weighed about 3¼ pounds and a bowl that weighed about 1¾ pounds, using the sanctuary standard. Both held fine flour mixed with oil, for the grain offering.
He also gave a gold dish of about 4 ounces, filled with incense.
The burnt offering consisted of one ram, one young bull, and one male yearling lamb.
For the sin offering there was a male goat.
For the peace offering he brought five rams and five billy goats, along with two oxen and five male lambs one year old. The gift belonged to Shelumiel son of Zurishaddai.
Next, on day six, Eliasaph son of Deuel approached for Gad’s tribe, of which he was leader.

He brought one silver plate weighing about 3¼ pounds and one silver bowl weighing about 1¾ pounds, measured by the sanctuary standard. Each was filled with fine flour mixed with oil as a grain offering.
There was a gold dish, about 4 ounces in weight, full of incense.
He gave a ram, a young bull, and a lamb, male and one year old, to be burned whole.
A male goat served as his sin offering.
He finished with a peace offering. It held two oxen, five rams, five billy goats, and five lambs, all male and each a year old. Eliasaph son of Deuel had given it.
Ephraim’s leader Elishama son of Ammihud offered his gift on day seven.
His gift included a silver plate of about 3¼ pounds and a silver bowl of about 1¾ pounds, both weighed by the sanctuary standard, and both filled with oil-mixed fine flour for a grain offering.
He added one gold dish weighing about 4 ounces, and it held incense.
His burnt offering: one young bull, one ram, and one year-old lamb, a male.
He added a billy goat as a sin offering.
The peace offering that Elishama son of Ammihud brought was made up of two oxen, five rams, five billy goats, and five yearling male lambs.
Gamaliel son of Pedahzur, head of the tribe of Manasseh, was the one who gave on the eighth day.
The silver he gave was a plate of about 3¼ pounds and a bowl of about 1¾ pounds, by the sanctuary’s weights. Fine flour mixed with oil filled both, to serve as a grain offering.
A gold dish of about 4 ounces, packed with incense, came as well.
To be burned whole, he supplied one male lamb a year old, one ram, and one young bull.
He gave a male goat for the sin offering.
His peace offering was two oxen, with five rams, five billy goats, and five male lambs a year old. Gamaliel son of Pedahzur presented all of it.
Benjamin’s tribal leader, Abidan son of Gideoni, made his presentation on day nine.
He presented a silver plate (about 3¼ pounds) and a silver bowl (about 1¾ pounds) by the sanctuary standard, each one full of fine flour and oil blended for a grain offering.
He added a gold dish that weighed about 4 ounces and was heaped with incense.
A young bull, a ram, and a male lamb in its first year were his burnt offering.
For the sin offering there was a male goat.
Peace offering: five rams, five billy goats, five yearling male lambs, and two oxen. That was what Abidan son of Gideoni offered.
Day ten brought Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai, the chief of Dan’s tribe, with his gift.

Two silver pieces came with him: a plate that weighed about 3¼ pounds and a bowl that weighed about 1¾ pounds, using the sanctuary standard. Both held fine flour mixed with oil, for the grain offering.
There was a gold dish, about 4 ounces in weight, full of incense.
The burnt offering consisted of one ram, one young bull, and one male yearling lamb.
A male goat served as his sin offering.
For the peace offering he brought five rams and five billy goats, along with two oxen and five male lambs one year old. The gift belonged to Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai.
On the eleventh day, Asher’s chief Pagiel son of Ochran stepped forward with his gift.

He brought one silver plate weighing about 3¼ pounds and one silver bowl weighing about 1¾ pounds, measured by the sanctuary standard. Each was filled with fine flour mixed with oil as a grain offering.
He added one gold dish weighing about 4 ounces, and it held incense.
He gave a ram, a young bull, and a lamb, male and one year old, to be burned whole.
He added a billy goat as a sin offering.
He finished with a peace offering. It held two oxen, five rams, five billy goats, and five lambs, all male and each a year old. Pagiel son of Ochran had given it.
Last came Ahira son of Enan, Naphtali’s leader, on the twelfth day, with his gift.
His gift included a silver plate of about 3¼ pounds and a silver bowl of about 1¾ pounds, both weighed by the sanctuary standard, and both filled with oil-mixed fine flour for a grain offering.
A gold dish of about 4 ounces, packed with incense, came as well.
His burnt offering: one young bull, one ram, and one year-old lamb, a male.
He gave a male goat for the sin offering.
The peace offering that Ahira son of Enan brought was made up of two oxen, five rams, five billy goats, and five yearling male lambs.
Israel’s leaders gave these gifts to dedicate the altar when it was anointed: silver plates (twelve), silver bowls (twelve), and gold dishes (twelve).
Every silver plate weighed about 3¼ pounds, and every bowl about 1¾ pounds. By the sanctuary standard, the silver in all these pieces totaled about 60 pounds.{e}
The twelve gold dishes full of incense weighed about 4 ounces each by the sanctuary standard, and the gold in all the dishes totaled about 3 pounds.{f}
Burnt offering: twelve bulls, twelve rams, and twelve male yearling lambs, with the grain offerings that go with them. For the sin offering, the leaders gave twelve male goats.
Peace offering: twenty-four bulls, sixty rams, sixty billy goats, and sixty yearling male lambs. All this was given to dedicate the altar after its anointing.

Whenever Moses went into the meeting tent to talk with Yahweh,{g} he would hear the voice addressing him from over the lid on the chest of the covenant, between the two winged creatures. That was how Yahweh spoke with him.

notes.text: Hebrew tsav, perhaps “covered” or “litter-like.” The meaning is uncertain.
Hebrew hanukkah, “dedication,” the word later used for the festival of the rededication of the temple in 164 BC. So also in verses 11, 84, and 88.

Hebrew “one silver plate, its weight a hundred thirty shekels, one silver bowl of seventy shekels,” about 3¼ pounds (1.5 kilograms) and 1¾ pounds (0.8 kilogram). A shekel was about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams); standards varied. On the sanctuary shekel, see Exodus 30:13. The same weights apply in each of the twelve offerings that follow.
Hebrew “ten shekels,” about 4 ounces (115 grams).
Hebrew “2,400 shekels,” about 60 pounds (27.6 kilograms).
Hebrew “ten shekels each ... 120 shekels,” about 4 ounces (115 grams) each and 3 pounds (1.4 kilograms) in all.
That is, with Yahweh. The Hebrew form translated “speaking” (middabber) is unusual; some interpreters take it to mean that the voice was speaking, as it were, to itself, with Moses overhearing.

verses.text: Yahweh told Moses,
“Say to Aaron: When you put the lamps in place, the seven of them are to light up the space ahead of the lampstand.”
Aaron did this. He set the lamps facing the front of the lampstand, just as Yahweh had ordered Moses.
The lampstand was made of gold, hammered into shape from its base up to its flowers. It followed the pattern Yahweh had shown Moses.
Yahweh told Moses,
“Select the Levites from among the Israelites and make them ritually clean.
Here is how you make them clean: splash water of purification{a} on them. They are to shave every hair on their bodies, launder their clothes, and so become clean.
Have them take a young bull, along with a grain offering of fine flour blended with oil. You are to take a different young bull for the sin offering.
Bring the Levites forward to the front of the meeting tent and call together the whole community of Israel.
When you bring the Levites before Yahweh, the Israelites are to place their hands on them.
Then Aaron is to present the Levites to Yahweh as a wave offering{b} on the Israelites’ behalf, so they may carry out Yahweh’s service.
The Levites then lay their hands on the bulls’ heads. You will offer one bull to Yahweh as a sin offering and the second as a burnt offering, to make things right for the Levites.
Stand the Levites before Aaron and his sons, and offer them up to Yahweh with a wave offering.
That is how you will set the Levites aside from all other Israelites. The Levites are mine.
After you have made them clean and presented them, the Levites may enter to serve in the meeting tent.
They are given to me completely, taken from the Israelites. I have claimed them for myself in place of every firstborn, the first child born to each Israelite mother.
All Israel’s firstborn belong to me, men and animals. On the day I killed Egypt’s firstborn, I set them aside as my own.
Now I have taken the Levites in place of all Israel’s firstborn.

Out of all the Israelites I have handed the Levites to Aaron and his sons as a gift. The Levites carry out the work of the Israelites at the meeting tent and make things right for them, so the people will not be struck by plague when they approach the holy place.”
Moses, Aaron, and all the Israelite community did this with the Levites, exactly as Yahweh had told Moses about them.
The Levites cleared themselves of sin and laundered their clothes. Then Aaron offered them to Yahweh as a wave offering and made things right for them to cleanse them.
Afterward the Levites went in to serve at the meeting tent, under the direction of Aaron and his sons. All was done to them as Yahweh had commanded Moses.
Yahweh told Moses,
“This is the rule for the Levites: a man of twenty-five or older joins the group that serves at the meeting tent.{c}
At fifty, he retires from the work and no longer serves.
He may help his fellow Levites in the meeting tent by guarding it, but he does no heavy work. That is how you are to assign the Levites’ duties.”

notes.text: Hebrew “water of sin,” that is, water that removes sin and impurity.
Hebrew tenufah, an offering formally presented before Yahweh, possibly with a lifting or waving motion.
Compare 4:3, where the age is thirty. The difference may reflect a period of apprenticeship or a change in practice. The Greek Old Testament has twenty-five in both places (4:3, 23, 30).

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses in the Wilderness of Sinai in the first month (March-April){a} of the second year after the Israelites had left Egypt. He said,
“Have the Israelites keep the Passover at the time set for it.
Keep it on the fourteenth day of this month (March-April), at twilight,{b} following all its rules and customs.”
Moses told the people of Israel it was time for the Passover.
They kept it at twilight on the fourteenth day of the first month (March-April), in the Wilderness of Sinai. The Israelites followed every order Yahweh had given Moses.
Some men, however, were unclean because of a dead body and could not keep the Passover that day. They went to Moses and Aaron that same day
They told Moses, “A dead person has made us unclean. Why must we miss out on presenting Yahweh’s offering on time with the other Israelites?”
Moses answered, “Wait here while I find out what Yahweh commands about you.”
Yahweh told Moses,
“Tell the Israelites: If any of you or your descendants become unclean by touching a corpse, or happen to be away on a distant journey, you can still keep Yahweh’s Passover.{c}
Keep it in the second month (April-May) at twilight on day fourteen, eating the lamb with bread without yeast and bitter herbs.
Do not save any of it until morning, and do not break any of its bones. Follow every rule for the Passover.
Anyone who is clean and at home, yet neglects the Passover, must be cut off from his people. He failed to bring Yahweh’s offering on time, and he will carry the guilt for his sin.
If a foreigner living among you wants to keep Yahweh’s Passover, he may, following its rules and customs. The same rule applies to the foreigner and the native-born.”
On the day the dwelling was set up, a cloud covered it, the tent that held the covenant. From evening until morning the cloud over the dwelling looked like fire.
It stayed that way all the time: the cloud covered it by day,{d} and the fire’s glow by night.
Each time the cloud lifted from above the tent, the Israelites moved out. They made camp at the spot where the cloud stopped.
They moved when Yahweh said to move and camped when Yahweh said to camp. As long as the cloud hung over the dwelling, they stayed in the camp.
Even when the cloud stayed over the dwelling for many days, the Israelites obeyed Yahweh and did not move on.
Other times the cloud remained over the dwelling just a few days. They camped at Yahweh’s command and moved on at Yahweh’s command.
At times the cloud stayed only from evening until morning, and when it rose in the morning, they moved. Or it might stay a day and a night, and they moved when it rose.
Whether the cloud stayed over the dwelling two days, a month, or a year,{e} the Israelites stayed in camp and did not travel. When it rose, they traveled.
At Yahweh’s word they camped, and at Yahweh’s word they moved. They followed Yahweh’s orders, which came through Moses.

notes.text: The first month of Israel’s religious calendar, which began in spring, was Abib, later called Nisan (Exodus 12:2; 13:4). Because the months followed the moon, the dates fall in different parts of March and April from year to year. This is one month before the census of 1:1.
Hebrew “between the two evenings,” probably the time between sunset and dark. So also in verses 5 and 11. See the note at Exodus 12:6.
This is the provision for a “second Passover” one month later, in the second month (Iyyar, also called Ziv).
The Greek Old Testament and other ancient versions read “by day.” The traditional Hebrew text lacks the words.
Hebrew yamim, “days,” which can mean a year or an indefinite period.

verses.text: Yahweh told Moses,
“Make two trumpets out of silver, hammered into shape. They will be used to call the community together and to signal the camps to move.
When you blow both, all the people are to assemble in front of you at the doorway of the meeting tent.
When only one is blown, just the leaders, the heads of Israel’s divisions,{a} are to gather before you.
When you blow a loud blast,{b} the camps on the east side move out.
When you blow a second loud blast, the camps on the south side move out. A loud blast is the signal each time they are to leave.{c}
To call the assembly together, blow the trumpets, but without the loud blast.
Aaron’s sons, the priests, are the ones to blow the trumpets. This rule is for you and your descendants for all time.
If you go to war in your homeland against an enemy who attacks you, sound the trumpets with a loud blast. Then Yahweh your God will bring you to mind and save you from your foes.

Blow the trumpets as well on days when you celebrate, at your festivals and at the start of each month.{d} Sound them over your burnt offerings and your peace offerings. They will bring you to your God’s mind. I am Yahweh your God.”{e}
On the twentieth day of the second month (April-May) in the second year,{f} the cloud lifted away from the dwelling that held the covenant.
The Israelites left the Wilderness of Sinai, going from one stopping place to the next. At last the cloud settled in the Wilderness of Paran.
This was their first march, and it followed Yahweh’s command given through Moses.
First in line, with their divisions, went the banner of Judah’s camp. Nahshon son of Amminadab led their army.
Nethanel son of Zuar led the army of Issachar’s tribe.
Eliab son of Helon led the army of Zebulun’s tribe.
After that the dwelling was dismantled, and the Gershonites and the Merarites, who were its carriers, moved out.
After them went the banner of Reuben’s camp, with their divisions. Elizur son of Shedeur led their army.
Shelumiel son of Zurishaddai led the army of Simeon’s tribe.
Eliasaph son of Deuel led the army of Gad’s tribe.
After them the Kohathites went, carrying the holy things. The dwelling would be put up again before they reached the new camp.
Following them went the banner of Ephraim’s camp, with their divisions. Elishama son of Ammihud led their army.
Gamaliel son of Pedahzur led the army of Manasseh’s tribe.
Abidan son of Gideoni led the army of Benjamin’s tribe.
Last of all, as the rear guard for every camp, went the banner of Dan’s camp, with their divisions. Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai led their army.
Pagiel son of Ochran led the army of Asher’s tribe.
Ahira son of Enan led the army of Naphtali’s tribe.
So the Israelites were arranged on the march, one division after another.

Moses spoke to Hobab, the son of Reuel{g} the Midianite and Moses’ father-in-law. “We are heading to the place Yahweh promised, when he said, ‘I will give it to you.’ Come with us and we will do right by you, because Yahweh has promised good to Israel.”
Hobab answered, “No, I won’t go. I’m going back to my own land and my own family.”
But Moses said, “Please stay with us. You know the wilderness campsites, and you can serve as our eyes.
If you come with us, we will share with you whatever good Yahweh gives us.”
So they left the mountain of Yahweh and traveled three days. The chest of Yahweh’s covenant went in front of them for those three days{h} to find a place for them to rest.
Yahweh’s cloud was above them by day whenever they left the camp.
Whenever the chest was lifted to travel,{i} Moses called out, “Get up, Yahweh! Scatter your enemies, and make those who hate you flee.”
And each time it came to rest, he said, “Come back, Yahweh, to Israel’s countless thousands.”{j}

notes.text: Or “clans.” See the note at 1:16.
Hebrew teru’ah, a loud blast or series of blasts, as distinct from an ordinary blowing of the trumpet.
The Greek Old Testament adds that at a third and a fourth blast the camps on the west and on the north are to set out. The Hebrew lacks this.
Hebrew “heads of your months,” the new moon at the beginning of each lunar month.

At this point the Samaritan Pentateuch adds a long passage taken from Deuteronomy 1:6-8, in which Yahweh commands Israel to leave Horeb and go into the hill country of the Amorites. Similar expansions, drawn from Deuteronomy or from elsewhere in Numbers, occur in the Samaritan Pentateuch at 12:16; 13:33; 14:40, 45; 20:13; 21; 27:23; and 31:20. Several are also preserved in fragments of Numbers from the Dead Sea Scrolls. They are not found in the traditional Hebrew text, and most are absent from the Greek Old Testament.

Second month: Iyyar, also called Ziv, of the spring-start religious calendar; because the months followed the moon, the date falls in different parts of April and May. Israel had been at Sinai about eleven months (Exodus 19:1).

Hobab means “beloved.” Reuel means “friend of God.” He is also called Jethro in Exodus 3:1; 18:1. Here it is not certain whether “Moses’ father-in-law” refers to Hobab or to Reuel; Judges 4:11 calls Hobab Moses’ father-in-law.
The repetition of “three days’ journey” is unusual; some interpreters suspect that the second occurrence arose from a copying error.

In the traditional Hebrew text, verses 35-36 are set off by a reversed Hebrew letter nun before and after them, the so-called “inverted nuns.” Ancient rabbis explained these marks as showing that the passage stands out of its proper place or forms a separate book. The Greek Old Testament places verse 34 after verses 35-36.
Or “Return, Yahweh, the countless thousands of Israel,” that is, bring them back. Hebrew “ten thousands of thousands.”

verses.text: Before long the people were complaining about their hardships where Yahweh could hear. His anger flared up, and a fire from Yahweh broke out among them, burning the far edges of the camp.
The people shouted for Moses. When he prayed to Yahweh, the fire went out.
That place was named Taberah,{a} because Yahweh’s fire had burned among them there.
The mixed crowd{b} traveling with Israel began to long for better food, and soon the Israelites were crying too. “Who will give us meat?” they said.
“We remember the fish we ate back in Egypt, and it cost us nothing! We had cucumbers and melons, leeks, onions, and garlic!
Now our strength is gone. Manna, and only manna, is all we have to look at!”
The manna looked like coriander seed, and its color was like that of bdellium.{c}

The people went around scooping it up. They ground it between millstones or pounded it in a mortar, then boiled it in a pot and formed it into flat cakes. The flavor was like a cake baked with olive oil.
Each night the manna came down on the camp along with the dew.
Moses heard the people crying, family after family, at the doors of their tents. Yahweh was furious, and Moses was troubled too.
He said to Yahweh, “Why have you brought trouble on your servant? What have I done to lose your favor, that you make me responsible for all these people?

Was I the one who conceived them? Was it I who gave them birth? Why do you tell me, ‘Hold them to your chest, as a nanny holds a nursing child, and walk them to the land you swore to give their ancestors’?
Where can I find meat for this entire people? They wail to me, ‘Give us meat so we can eat!’
I cannot bear the weight of this whole nation by myself. It is more than I can manage.
If this is how you plan to treat me, then please kill me now, if I have any favor with you at all. Spare me from seeing my own ruin.”{d}
Yahweh said to Moses, “Gather seventy of Israel’s elders for me, men you recognize as elders and officers over the people. Lead them to the meeting tent so they can take their places beside you.
There I will come down and speak with you. I will remove part of the Spirit{e} resting on you and place it on them, so they can share the load of these people and you are not carrying it by yourself.

Say to the people: Set yourselves apart for tomorrow. You are going to have meat. Yahweh listened while you wailed, ‘If only we had meat! Life was better in Egypt!’ So Yahweh is giving you meat, and you will eat it.
It will last longer than a day or two. It will last longer than five days, ten days, or twenty.
You will eat meat for a month, until it comes out your nose and makes you sick. This is because you refused Yahweh, who is among you, and wailed in front of him, ‘Why did we ever leave Egypt?’”
Moses said, “I am among 600,000 men on foot,{f} and yet you promise, ‘I will give them meat for a month.’
Could enough sheep and cattle be killed to satisfy them? Could every fish in the sea be caught to satisfy them?”
Yahweh replied, “Has Yahweh’s arm grown short?{g} You will see now whether what I say happens or not.”
Moses went out and passed on Yahweh’s words to the people. He collected seventy of the people’s elders and had them take positions around the tent.

Yahweh descended in the cloud and spoke with Moses. He took some of the Spirit that was on Moses and placed it on the seventy elders. When the Spirit settled on them, they spoke as prophets, but they never did it again.{h}

Two of the men were still in the camp, one named Eldad and the other Medad.{i} Their names were on the list, but they had not gone out to the tent. Even so, the Spirit settled on them, and they prophesied there in the camp.
A boy ran to Moses with the news: “Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp!”
Joshua son of Nun, who had assisted Moses from his youth,{j} spoke up: “Moses, my lord, stop them!”
But Moses replied, “Are you jealous on my account? How I wish all of Yahweh’s people were prophets, with Yahweh giving his Spirit to every one of them!”
Then Moses and Israel’s elders went back to the camp.
A wind sent by Yahweh drove quail in from the sea and dropped them around the camp, a day’s walk in every direction. They lay about 3 feet{k} deep on the ground.
The people spent that whole day, the night, and the next day gathering the quail. Nobody gathered less than about 60 bushels.{l} They laid them out to dry all around the camp.
While the meat was still between their teeth, before they could swallow it, Yahweh’s anger flared against the people, and he struck them with a terrible plague.
That place was named Kibroth-hattaavah,{m} because the people who had craved meat were buried there.
From Kibroth-hattaavah the people moved on to Hazeroth, where they remained.

notes.text: Taberah means “burning.”
Hebrew ‘asafsuf, a rare word for a gathered crowd, probably the non-Israelites who left Egypt with them (Exodus 12:38).
Hebrew bedolakh, probably a pale, translucent resin. Compare Genesis 2:12.
Ancient scribal tradition lists this as one of the “corrections of the scribes”: the text originally read “your misery” (that is, the wrong done to Moses by Yahweh), and was changed out of reverence.
Or “spirit.” So also in verses 25, 26, and 29.
The round figure corresponds to the census total of 603,550 (1:46). On the meaning of the figures, see the note at 1:46.
That is, is Yahweh’s power limited?
Or “but they did not stop.” The Hebrew verb is ambiguous; the Targums and the Latin Vulgate read “and they did not cease.”
Eldad means “God has loved.” Medad perhaps means “beloved.”
Or “one of his chosen men.” The Greek Old Testament reads “the chosen one.”
Or “about two cubits deep,” meaning that the quail flew about 3 feet (90 centimeters) above the ground, or that they lay in heaps of that depth. A cubit was about 18 inches (45 centimeters).
Hebrew “ten homers,” about 60 bushels (2,200 liters). A homer was about 6 bushels (220 liters); standards varied.
Kibroth-hattaavah means “graves of craving.”

verses.text: Miriam and Aaron criticized Moses because of the Cushite{a} wife he had taken. He had indeed married a Cushite.
“Is Moses the only one Yahweh has spoken through?” they said. “Hasn’t he spoken through us as well?” And Yahweh heard them.
Moses, for his part, was extremely humble,{b} more so than any other person on the earth.
All at once Yahweh said to Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, “You three, step out to the meeting tent.” So they went.
Yahweh descended in a pillar of cloud, took his stand at the tent’s entrance, and summoned Aaron and Miriam. Both came forward.
He said, “Hear this. If you have a prophet, I, Yahweh, show myself to him in visions, and I talk to him in dreams.
It is different with my servant Moses. He is trusted with my entire household.
With him I talk directly, in plain speech rather than puzzles, and he looks on the form of Yahweh. Why were you not afraid to speak against Moses, my servant?”
Yahweh’s anger blazed against them, and he left.
As the cloud lifted from the tent, there stood Miriam, covered with a skin disease, white as snow.{c} Aaron turned and saw her, diseased.
He said to Moses, “Please, my lord, do not make us pay for this sin. We acted foolishly and did wrong.
Do not let her be like a baby born dead, with half its flesh already decayed.”{d}
Moses called out to Yahweh, “Heal her, God, I beg you!”
Yahweh told Moses, “Suppose her father had spat in her face. Would she not bear the disgrace for a week? Let her stay outside the camp for seven days, and then she may return.”
Miriam stayed outside the camp for seven days, and the people did not march until she was readmitted.
After this the people set out from Hazeroth and camped in the Wilderness of Paran.{e}

notes.text: Cush was the region south of Egypt (ancient Nubia). Some identify the woman with Zipporah, whose people were from Midian (Exodus 2:21), linking Cush with Cushan (Habakkuk 3:7); others think of a second wife.
Or “meek.” Hebrew ‘anav, one who is lowly and dependent on God rather than self-assertive.
That is, flaky or white like snow. On the Hebrew term for skin disease, see the note at 5:2.
Ancient scribal tradition lists “her mother’s womb ... her flesh” here as a “correction of the scribes” for an original “our mother’s womb ... our flesh.”
At this point the Samaritan Pentateuch adds material drawn from Deuteronomy 1:20-23, introducing the sending of the spies. See the note at 10:10.

verses.text: Yahweh said to Moses,
“Dispatch some men to spy out Canaan, the land I am giving to the Israelites. From every tribe of their ancestors, choose one man who is a chief.”
At Yahweh’s order, Moses sent them out from the Wilderness of Paran. All of them were heads of the Israelite tribes.
Their names were these. Reuben’s man was Shammua son of Zaccur.
Simeon’s was Shaphat son of Hori.
Judah’s was Caleb son of Jephunneh.{a}
Issachar’s was Igal son of Joseph.
Ephraim’s was Hoshea son of Nun.
Benjamin’s was Palti son of Raphu.
Zebulun’s was Gaddiel son of Sodi.
For Joseph’s tribe of Manasseh it was Gaddi son of Susi.
Dan’s was Ammiel son of Gemalli.
Asher’s was Sethur son of Michael.
Naphtali’s was Nahbi son of Vophsi.
Gad’s was Geuel son of Machi.
Those were the men Moses sent to spy on the land. (Moses renamed Hoshea son of Nun as Joshua.{b})
Moses sent them to spy on Canaan and instructed them, “Head up through the Negev{c} and into the hills.
Observe the country. Are its people mighty or weak, many or few?
Is the land where they live good or bad? Are their towns unwalled camps or strongholds?
Is the soil rich or thin? Does it have forests? Take courage, and carry back some of what grows there.” The season was the first ripening of grapes.{d}
They went up and surveyed the land, starting at the Wilderness of Zin and reaching to Rehob at Lebo-hamath.{e}
They went up through the Negev and came to Hebron. Living there were Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, Anak’s descendants.{f} (Hebron was founded seven years earlier than Zoan in Egypt.)
When they reached the Valley of Eshcol,{g} they cut down a vine branch bearing one cluster of grapes. Two men had to lift it on a pole between them. They gathered pomegranates and figs as well.
Because of that cluster the Israelites cut there, the spot was named the Valley of Eshcol.
After forty days of exploring, the men came back.
They returned to Moses, Aaron, and all the Israelite people, who were at Kadesh in the Wilderness of Paran. The scouts reported to them all and displayed the produce of the land.
They said to Moses, “We reached the land you sent us to explore. Milk and honey really do flow there! Look at its fruit.
But the people living there are powerful, and their cities are huge and well defended. We even saw descendants of Anak there.
Amalekites live in the Negev. Hittites, Jebusites, and Amorites live in the hill country. Canaanites live along the sea and beside the Jordan.”
Caleb calmed the people gathered around Moses. “Let’s go up at once and seize it,” he said. “We are well able to take it.”
The men who had traveled with him disagreed. “We can’t go against those people,” they said. “They are too strong for us.”
They gave the Israelites a discouraging account of the land they had explored. “The country we crossed to explore it swallows up those who settle there,” they said. “Everybody we saw was enormous.
We saw the Nephilim{h} there (Anak’s descendants come from the Nephilim). Next to them we felt like grasshoppers, and that is how we looked to them.”{i}

notes.text: Many names in this list are found only here; their meanings are uncertain. Caleb may mean “dog,” perhaps in the sense of a faithful servant. Shammua means “heard”; Shaphat, “he has judged”; Igal, “he redeems”; Hoshea, “salvation”; Gaddiel, “God is my fortune”; Ammiel, “my kinsman is God”; Michael, “who is like God?”
Hoshea means “salvation.” Joshua (Hebrew Yehoshua’) means “Yahweh is salvation.”
Hebrew negev, “dry land,” the arid region in the south of Canaan.
That is, July-August.
Or “Lebo of Hamath,” or “the entrance of Hamath,” at the northern limit of the land.
Or “the Anakim,” a people remembered for their great height. The name Anak may mean “long-necked.” Ahiman perhaps means “my brother is a gift”; Sheshai and Talmai are of uncertain meaning.
Eshcol means “cluster.”
Hebrew nefilim, perhaps “fallen ones.” Compare Genesis 6:4. The Greek Old Testament translates “giants.”
At this point the Samaritan Pentateuch adds material drawn from Deuteronomy 1:27-33. See the note at 10:10.

verses.text: That night the whole community raised a great wail, and the people wept.
Israelites everywhere grumbled at Moses and Aaron. As one voice the community cried, “If only we had died back in Egypt, or out here in this desert!
Why would Yahweh march us into that country only to have us cut down by swords? Our wives and children will become spoils of war. Going home to Egypt would be better!”
Then they began saying to one another, “We need a new commander. Let’s turn around for Egypt.”
Moses and Aaron threw themselves to the ground in front of the whole Israelite assembly.
Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh had both been among the scouts. They ripped their robes in sorrow
They told the whole community of Israel, “The land we crossed to explore is wonderfully good.
If Yahweh is happy with us, he will bring us in and give us that country, a land flowing with milk and honey.
Just do not turn against Yahweh. And do not fear the people there. We will swallow them up! Their protection{a} has left them, and Yahweh is on our side. Do not be afraid of them.”
But the whole community was talking about throwing stones at them. Just then Yahweh’s glory appeared at the meeting tent for all the Israelites to see.
Yahweh asked Moses, “How long will this people treat me with contempt? How long will they refuse to trust me, despite every sign I have performed among them?
I will strike them with a plague and wipe them out. Then I will make you into a nation larger and mightier than theirs.”
Moses said to Yahweh, “The Egyptians will hear about this, since you used your power to bring these people out from among them.

Then they will pass it on to the inhabitants of this land. Those people already know that you, Yahweh, live among this people. They know that people see you face to face, that your cloud stands over them, and that you walk ahead of them in a pillar of cloud during the day and a pillar of fire at night.
Suppose you wipe out this whole people in a single blow. Then every nation that has heard your reputation will say,
‘Yahweh was too weak to get these people into the country he swore to give them. That is why he butchered them in the desert.’
So now, my Lord, show the greatness of your power,{b} as you said:

‘Yahweh is slow to anger and overflowing with faithful love.{c} He forgives wrongdoing and rebellion, but he does not let the guilty go unpunished, and he holds children accountable for their parents’ wrongdoing to the third and fourth generation.’
Because your faithful love is so great, pardon the guilt of this people, as you have pardoned them all the way from Egypt until today.”
Yahweh answered, “Because you asked, I pardon them.
But I swear by my life, and by the way Yahweh’s glory will fill the whole earth,
Not one of the people who witnessed my glory, along with the signs I performed in Egypt and the desert, yet put me to the test ten times and would not listen to me,
not one will set eyes on the country I vowed to their forefathers. Whoever spurned me will never see it.
My servant Caleb is different. His spirit is not like theirs, and he has followed me with his whole heart. I will bring him into the land he walked through, and his children will possess it.
The Amalekites and Canaanites live in the valleys, so tomorrow turn around and head into the wilderness toward the Red Sea.”{d}
Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron:
“How much longer will this wicked community keep complaining about me? The Israelites’ grumbling against me has reached my ears.
Tell them: As surely as I live, says Yahweh, I will do to you exactly what I heard you say.
Here in this desert your bodies will fall, all of you who were registered, from age twenty up, because you complained about me.
Not one of you will go into the country where I promised{e} to settle you, apart from Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun.
Your little ones, the ones you said would be carried off, I will bring in. They will come to know the land you rejected.
You, though, will be the ones whose bodies drop in this desert.
Your children will be shepherds in the wilderness for forty years. They will carry the cost of your unfaithfulness{f} until the last of you has died out there.
You explored the land for forty days. For each day, one year: forty years you will pay for your wrongdoing, and you will find out what it is like to have me as your opponent.{g}
I, Yahweh, have spoken. I will certainly do this to this whole wicked community that has joined together against me. They will come to an end in this wilderness, and here they will die.”
Moses had sent men to scout the land. They had come back and made the whole community complain about him by spreading a bad report about the land.
Those men who gave the bad report about the land were struck dead by a plague in front of Yahweh.
Of all the men sent to scout the country, only Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh stayed alive.
Moses told the Israelites all that Yahweh had said, and the people were crushed with sorrow.
First thing the next morning, they started up toward the high hill country, saying, “Here we are! We will go where Yahweh said, for we admit we sinned.”{h}
Moses said, “Why are you disobeying Yahweh’s order? This will not work.
Do not go up there, because Yahweh is not with you. Your enemies will defeat you.
The Amalekites and Canaanites will meet you there, and you will die by the sword. You have turned away from Yahweh, so Yahweh will not be with you.”
They pushed ahead anyway toward the top of the hill country, even though neither the chest of Yahweh’s covenant nor Moses left the camp.
Then the Amalekites and Canaanites who lived in those hills came down, attacked them, and beat them back all the way to Hormah.{i}

notes.text: Hebrew “their shadow,” that is, the protection of their gods.
In the traditional Hebrew text the first letter of the word for “be great” is written larger than normal, a scribal feature with no certain meaning.
Hebrew khesed, covenant loyalty and love. Verses 18-19 echo Exodus 34:6-7.
Hebrew yam suf, “Sea of Reeds.” Here it probably refers to the Gulf of Aqaba. See the note at Exodus 10:19.
Hebrew “lifted my hand,” a gesture of swearing an oath.
Hebrew “bear your whoredoms,” a common biblical image for unfaithfulness to God.
Or “what it means to have me against you.” The Hebrew word is rare.
At this point and after verse 45 the Samaritan Pentateuch adds material drawn from Deuteronomy 1-2. See the note at 10:10.
Hormah means “destruction” or “devoted to destruction.” Compare 21:3.

verses.text: Yahweh told Moses,
“Tell the Israelites: After you enter the land I am giving you to live in,

you may bring Yahweh a gift made by fire from your cattle or flock, to produce a smell that pleases him. It may be a burnt offering or another sacrifice, whether you are keeping a vow, giving a freewill gift, or celebrating one of your festivals.
Whoever brings the gift must also bring Yahweh a grain offering of about 2 quarts of fine flour mixed with about 1 quart of oil.{a}
With each lamb, for a burnt offering or another sacrifice, prepare about 1 quart of wine to pour out.
With each ram, prepare a grain offering of about 4 quarts of fine flour mixed with about 1⅓ quarts of oil.{b}
For the drink offering, bring about 1⅓ quarts of wine, a smell that pleases Yahweh.
Suppose you prepare a young bull as a burnt offering or other sacrifice, to keep a vow or as a peace offering to Yahweh.
Along with the bull, bring a grain offering of about 6 quarts of fine flour mixed with about 2 quarts of oil.{c}
And for the drink offering, bring about 2 quarts of wine. It is a gift made by fire, a smell that pleases Yahweh.
Follow these rules for every ox, ram, lamb, or young goat.
However many animals you prepare, do the same for each one.
Every native-born Israelite must follow these rules whenever he brings a gift made by fire that pleases Yahweh.

Suppose a foreigner is staying with you, or anyone else living among you in later generations, and he wishes to present a gift made by fire with a smell that pleases Yahweh. He is to follow your practice exactly.
The assembly will have a single rule, for you and for the outsider living with you. This rule lasts through all your generations. Before Yahweh, the outsider is the same as you.
The same law and the same ruling apply to you and to the foreigner living with you.”
Yahweh told Moses,
“Tell the Israelites: When you reach the land where I am taking you,
and begin to eat the food it produces, set aside a portion for Yahweh.
Offer a loaf from the first of your dough{d} as a contribution, the same way you set aside a share of the grain from the threshing floor.
In every generation, give Yahweh a contribution from the first of your dough.
“Now suppose you fail by mistake and do not keep every one of the commands Yahweh gave Moses,
everything Yahweh ordered through Moses, from the day he gave the order and in all the generations after,

and suppose it happens by mistake, without the community knowing. The whole community must then offer one young bull as a burnt offering, with its grain offering and drink offering as required, to produce a smell that pleases Yahweh, and one male goat as a sin offering.

Through the priest, the entire Israelite community will have their wrong made right and be pardoned, since it was done in error. They are to bring Yahweh their gift made by fire and their sin offering to answer for the error.
Pardon will reach the whole Israelite community and the outsiders living with them, since the entire nation shared in the error.
“If just one person sins by mistake, he must offer a year-old female goat as a sin offering.
The priest will make things right before Yahweh for the person who erred, and he will be pardoned.
The same law applies to everyone who sins by mistake, whether native-born Israelite or foreigner living among them.
But the person who sins on purpose,{e} native or foreign-born, is spitting in Yahweh’s face. That one is to be removed from his people.
That person has despised Yahweh’s word and broken his command, and must be cut off completely. The guilt stays on him.”
While the Israelites were in the wilderness, some people found a man picking up wood on the Sabbath.
Those who caught him led him to Moses, Aaron, and everyone gathered there.
They kept him under guard, since it had not been decided what to do with him.
Yahweh said to Moses, “That man is to be executed. Everyone in the community must pelt him with stones beyond the edge of the camp.”
So the whole group marched him out past the edge of the camp and pelted him with stones until he was dead, exactly as Yahweh had told Moses.
Yahweh told Moses,
“Tell the Israelites to sew tassels{f} on the corners of their clothes, in every generation, with a blue{g} cord in the tassel at each corner.
When you look at the tassels, you will remember all Yahweh’s commands and obey them, rather than chasing after what your own heart and eyes want, which leads you into unfaithfulness.
Then you will remember my commands and obey them all, and you will belong fully to your God.
I am Yahweh your God, who rescued you from Egypt so that I could be your God. I am Yahweh your God.”

notes.text: Hebrew “a tenth of fine flour mixed with a quarter of a hin of oil,” about 2.2 liters of flour and 0.9 liter of oil. The tenth is a tenth of an ephah; an ephah was about three-fifths of a bushel (22 liters), and a hin about 1 gallon (3.7 liters). Standards varied. So also with the wine in verse 5.
Hebrew “two-tenths of fine flour mixed with a third of a hin of oil,” about 4.4 liters of flour and 1.2 liters of oil. So also with the wine in verse 7.
Hebrew “three-tenths of fine flour mixed with half a hin of oil,” about 6.6 liters of flour and 1.9 liters of oil. So also with the wine in verse 10.
Or “coarse meal.” The Hebrew word ‘arisah is uncertain.
That is, defiantly and deliberately. Hebrew “with a high hand.”
Hebrew tsitsit, a tassel or fringe.
Hebrew tekhelet, a blue or violet dye made from murex shellfish.

subheads.1: Offerings with flour, oil, and wine

verses.text: Korah son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, took action,{a} along with Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, and On son of Peleth, all from the tribe of Reuben.{b}
They confronted Moses, backed by 250 other Israelites, well-known community leaders who had been chosen as members of the assembly.

They crowded around Moses and Aaron and said, “That’s enough from you two! The whole community is holy, each and every person, and Yahweh lives among them. What gives you the right to lift yourselves above Yahweh’s assembly?”
When Moses heard this, he fell facedown.

Then he told Korah and all his followers, “In the morning Yahweh will show who belongs to him and who is holy, and he will bring that person near to himself. The one he chooses will be the one he brings near.
Here is what to do, Korah, you and all your followers: take fire pans,
Light fires in them tomorrow and put incense on top before Yahweh. Whichever man Yahweh picks is the one who is holy. It is you sons of Levi who have overreached!”
Then Moses spoke to Korah again. “Hear me, sons of Levi:
Is it not enough for you that Israel’s God separated you from the rest of the community, brought you close to himself to work in Yahweh’s dwelling, and set you before the community to serve them?
He has brought you close, you and all your fellow Levites. Now you want the priesthood too?
It is Yahweh you are all conspiring against, not us. Aaron is nobody. Why do you grumble at him?”
Moses summoned Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab. They answered, “We refuse to come.
Is it a small thing that you pulled us out of a country flowing with milk and honey, just to have us die in the desert? Must you also appoint yourself our ruler?
