You have not brought us to a land flowing with milk and honey, or given us fields and vineyards to own. Do you want to put out these men’s eyes?{c} We will not come.”
This made Moses furious. He prayed to Yahweh, “Do not accept what they bring. Not once did I take a donkey from them, nor did I do harm to any one of them.”
Moses told Korah, “Tomorrow you and all your followers are to stand before Yahweh, with Aaron.
Each man must take his fire pan and put incense in it, then bring it before Yahweh: 250 fire pans. You and Aaron must each bring yours too.”
So every man picked up his fire pan, lit it, added incense, and took his place beside Moses and Aaron at the doorway of the meeting tent.
By then Korah had rallied the whole community to oppose them at the tent’s doorway. And the glory of Yahweh showed itself to everyone present.
Yahweh said to Moses and Aaron,
“Step away from this community, and I will destroy them in an instant.”
They fell with their faces to the ground and pleaded, “God, you give breath to every living creature. If one man sins, will you rage against this whole community?”
Yahweh told Moses,
“Order the community to get away from the homes of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram.”
Moses rose and hurried over to Dathan and Abiram, and the elders of Israel went behind him.
Moses cautioned everyone: “Back away from the tents of these wicked men, I beg you. Do not touch a single thing of theirs, or you will be carried off in all their sins.”

The people retreated from the homes of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. Dathan and Abiram stepped outside and stood at their tent entrances, together with their wives, their sons and daughters, and their little children.
Moses said, “This is how you will know that Yahweh sent me to do all these things, and that I did not make them up myself.{d}
If these men die a natural death like everyone else, then Yahweh did not send me.

But suppose Yahweh does something never seen before. Suppose the ground opens wide and swallows them and all that is theirs, and they drop alive into Sheol.{e} Then you will know that these men treated Yahweh with scorn.”
Moses had barely said the last word when the ground beneath the rebels split open.
The earth opened its mouth and swallowed them, along with their families and all of Korah’s followers{f} and everything they owned.
They went down alive into Sheol with all they had. The earth closed over them, and they vanished from the assembly.
All the Israelites around them ran when they heard the screams, shouting, “The earth will swallow us too!”
Then a fire went out from Yahweh and consumed the 250 men who had been presenting incense.
Yahweh told Moses,{g}
“Tell Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, to pick the fire pans out of the blaze and scatter the coals far away, because the pans are holy.

Take the fire pans of these men who forfeited their lives by their sin, and beat them into flat sheets to overlay the altar. Since they were presented to Yahweh, they are holy, and they will warn the Israelites.”
Eleazar the priest collected the bronze fire pans that the burned men had brought, and had them hammered into a covering for the altar.

This was a reminder to the Israelites that no outsider, no one who is not a descendant of Aaron, may come to burn incense before Yahweh, or he will end up like Korah and his followers. It was just as Yahweh had told Eleazar through Moses.
But on the following day, the entire Israelite community grumbled at Moses and Aaron again. “You two have killed Yahweh’s people!” they cried.
The crowd gathered against Moses and Aaron, but as they faced the meeting tent, they saw the cloud covering it and the glory of Yahweh appearing.
Moses and Aaron stepped up in front of the tent,
and Yahweh said to Moses,
“Get away from this community so I can destroy them in an instant.” Moses and Aaron fell facedown.

Moses said to Aaron, “Grab your fire pan, fill it with coals from the altar, and lay incense on them. Go quickly to the community and make things right for them, because Yahweh’s anger has broken out and a plague is under way.”
Aaron obeyed Moses and ran into the crowd. The plague was already spreading among the people. He added the incense and made things right for them.
Standing between the dead and the living, he held back the plague.
The plague killed 14,700 people, in addition to those who died because of Korah.
With the plague over, Aaron went back to Moses at the doorway of the meeting tent.

notes.text: Or “took men,” or “became insolent.” The Hebrew has no object, and the meaning is uncertain.
Korah perhaps means “bald.” Izhar means “shining.” Dathan is of uncertain meaning. Abiram means “my father is exalted.” On means “strength” or “wealth.” Peleth perhaps means “swiftness.”
That is, will you blind them to what you are doing?
Hebrew “from my heart.”
Sheol is the realm of the dead, pictured as beneath the earth. So also in verse 33.
According to 26:11, the sons of Korah did not die.
In the Hebrew text, verses 36-50 are numbered 17:1-15.

verses.text: Yahweh told Moses,{a}
“Tell the Israelites to bring you a staff from each ancestral family, taken from all their leaders: twelve in total. Inscribe every man’s name on his staff.
Levi’s staff gets Aaron’s name, because each head of an ancestral family gets one staff.
Lay them down inside the meeting tent in front of the covenant, the place where I meet with you.
The staff belonging to the man I choose will sprout. That will put an end to the Israelites’ constant complaining against you that reaches my ears.”
Moses spoke to the Israelites, and every leader handed him a staff, one for each ancestral family, twelve staffs. Aaron’s staff was among them.
Moses placed the staffs in front of Yahweh in the tent that held the covenant.
The next day Moses went into the tent, and Aaron’s staff, representing the house of Levi, had sprouted. It had buds, blossoms, and ripe almonds.
Moses carried all the staffs out from Yahweh’s presence to the Israelites. They looked at them, and each man picked up his own.
Yahweh told Moses, “Put Aaron’s staff back in front of the covenant, to be kept as a sign for these rebels. It will end their complaining against me, so they will not die.”
Moses did exactly what Yahweh had ordered.
The Israelites cried out to Moses, “We are doomed! We are finished, all of us!
Anyone who comes near Yahweh’s dwelling will die. Are we all going to die?”

notes.text: In the Hebrew text, verses 1-13 are numbered 17:16-28.

verses.text: Yahweh told Aaron, “You, your sons, and your whole family line share the responsibility for any wrong connected with the holy place. You and your sons alone answer for wrongs connected with the priesthood.
Bring along your relatives from Levi, your father’s tribe, so they can attach themselves to you{a} and assist you whenever you and your sons minister before the covenant tent.
The Levites will see to your needs and the care of the entire tent. They may never touch the objects inside the holy place or the altar, or death will come to them and to you.
They will be attached to you and look after the meeting tent, handling all of its work. No outsider is allowed near you.
You alone will watch over the holy place and the altar. Then my fury will never strike the Israelites again.
I have chosen your relatives the Levites from among the Israelites myself. They are a gift to you, dedicated to Yahweh for the work of the meeting tent.

You and your sons must handle your priestly duties yourselves, everything that has to do with the altar and the space behind the curtain. This is service I give you as a gift. Any outsider who comes near is to be executed.”
Yahweh also spoke to Aaron: “I have personally given you charge over the offerings reserved for me, the sacred gifts from all the Israelites. They are your portion,{b} and your sons’ permanent share.
Part of what is most holy and not burned is yours: every offering they bring me, whether grain offering, sin offering, or guilt offering. These are most holy, and they belong to you and your sons.
Eat them in a most holy place. Any male may eat them. Treat them as holy.

These are yours as well: whatever the Israelites set aside, including each wave offering. I hand these over to you, to your sons, and to your daughters, as a share for all time. Any member of your household who is clean can eat them.
I also give you the best of the olive oil, the new wine, and the grain, the first part of the harvest that they give to Yahweh.
The earliest ripe produce from their land, which they carry to Yahweh, is yours. Any clean member of your household may eat it.
Whatever in Israel is set apart for God{c} belongs to you.
The first offspring of every womb, human or animal, that is presented to Yahweh is yours. But you must always buy back the firstborn son, and the firstborn of unclean animals as well.
When a child is one month old, set his price for buying him back at about 2 ounces of silver,{d} using the standard of the holy place.
The firstborn of a cow, sheep, or goat must not be bought back. They are holy. Splash their blood on the altar and burn the fat as a gift made by fire, a smell that pleases Yahweh.
Their meat is yours, like the breast and right thigh that are lifted up in offering.

Every holy contribution the Israelites lift up to Yahweh, I give to you, your sons, and your daughters as a share for all time. It is an unbreakable agreement,{e} a covenant before Yahweh for you and your descendants.”
Yahweh said to Aaron, “You will have no land as an inheritance in their country and no territory among them. I myself am your share and your inheritance among the Israelites.
“To the Levites I give all the tenth-part gifts in Israel as their inheritance, as payment for their labor at the meeting tent.
From now on, the other Israelites must not approach the meeting tent. If they do, they will carry the guilt and die.
Only the Levites will do the labor at the meeting tent and answer for their own wrongs. This is a law for every generation. Land will never be allotted to them among the Israelites.
Instead, I give the Levites the tenth that the Israelites bring to Yahweh as a contribution. This is the reason I told them they would hold no land among the Israelites.”
Yahweh told Moses,
“Tell the Levites: When you collect from the Israelites the tenth I am giving you as your inheritance, you must offer a tenth of that tenth to Yahweh as a contribution.
Yahweh will count your contribution as though you had brought fresh grain from the threshing floor or juice from the winepress.
Likewise, from each tenth you receive from the Israelites, you will give Yahweh a contribution. Yahweh’s portion goes to Aaron the priest.
From everything you receive, set aside each contribution owed to Yahweh, taking the best and holiest part.
Say to the Levites: Once you have set aside the best part, the rest will count for you as produce from the threshing floor or winepress.
You and your households may consume it wherever you like. It is your wages for working at the meeting tent.
You will not be guilty if you have set aside the best part. But do not treat the Israelites’ holy gifts as ordinary, or you will die.”

notes.text: The Hebrew word for “join” (lavah) sounds like the name Levi. So also in verse 4.
Or “because of the anointing.” The Hebrew word is uncertain.
Hebrew kherem, something given to God permanently, either for destruction or for use in the sanctuary.
Hebrew “five shekels,” about 2 ounces (57 grams). A shekel was about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams); standards varied. The text says a shekel is twenty gerahs.
Hebrew “a covenant of salt.” Salt preserves, so the phrase means a lasting, binding agreement.

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron:
“Here is a rule that Yahweh has ordered. Tell the Israelites to bring you a red cow{a} with no defect or blemish, one that has never worn a yoke.
Give it to Eleazar the priest. Someone will take it out beyond the camp and slaughter it as he looks on.
Eleazar the priest will dip his finger in some of the blood and flick it seven times toward the front of the meeting tent.
While he watches, the cow will be burned whole: its skin, meat, blood, and dung.
The priest will throw cedar wood, hyssop, and red yarn onto the burning cow.
After that, the priest washes his clothes and bathes in water. Then he may come back into the camp, though he remains unclean until evening.
Whoever does the burning also has to wash his clothes and bathe in water. He is unclean until evening too.
A clean man will gather up the cow’s ashes and put them in a clean place outside the camp. The community will keep them for making the cleansing water,{b} which removes sin.
The man who gathers the ashes must wash his clothes and stays unclean until evening. This rule is permanent, for the Israelites and for foreigners living among them.
“Anyone who touches a human corpse is unclean for seven days.
He must cleanse himself with the water on the third day and the seventh day, and then he will be clean. If he skips cleansing on the third and seventh days, he stays unclean.
Whoever touches a dead body and does not cleanse himself pollutes Yahweh’s dwelling. That person must be cut off from Israel. The cleansing water was never sprinkled on him, so he remains unclean.
“Here is the rule for a death inside a tent. Everyone who walks in, and everyone who was already there, is unclean for seven days.
Any open jar without a cover tied on it is unclean.
Out in an open field, anyone who touches a man killed by a sword, a body that died naturally, a human bone, or a grave, is unclean for a week.
To cleanse an unclean person, put some ash from the burned sin offering into a jar and pour fresh running water{c} over it.

A clean man will then dip hyssop in the water and sprinkle it on the tent, all the things in it, and the people who were there. He also sprinkles anyone who touched a bone, a murdered or naturally dead body, or a grave.

The clean man sprinkles the unclean person on the third day and on the seventh day. On the seventh day he declares him clean. The person washes his clothes and bathes in water, and that evening he is clean.

“But a man who is unclean and refuses to be cleansed must be cut off from the assembly, because he has polluted Yahweh’s holy place. The cleansing water was not sprinkled on him, and he remains unclean.
This is a permanent rule for them. The man who sprinkles the water must wash his clothes, and whoever handles the water is unclean until evening.
Whatever an unclean person handles becomes unclean, and whoever touches that is unclean until evening.”

notes.text: Or “a red heifer.” The Hebrew word parah means a young female of the herd. Its reddish-brown color may call blood to mind.
Hebrew me niddah, “water of impurity,” used to remove uncleanness. So also in verses 13, 20, and 21.
Hebrew “living water,” meaning water from a flowing source.

subheads.11: Cleansing from contact with the dead

verses.text: In the first month (March-April),{a} the whole Israelite community arrived in the Zin Desert and settled at Kadesh. There Miriam died and was buried.
The community had no water, so they gathered against Moses and Aaron.
They argued with Moses: “We wish we had died along with our brothers in front of Yahweh!
Why did you haul Yahweh’s assembly out to this desert to die, us and our animals alike?
Why drag us out of Egypt to this terrible place? There is no grain here, no figs, no grapes, no pomegranates, and not even water to drink!”
Moses and Aaron walked away from the crowd to the doorway of the meeting tent and dropped to the ground on their faces. Yahweh’s glory then showed itself to them.
Yahweh told Moses,

“Take the staff. You and your brother Aaron are to gather the community. Then, with everyone watching, tell the rock to yield its water. Out of the rock you will draw enough for the people and their livestock to drink.”
Moses took the staff from where it lay in front of Yahweh, just as he was told.
Moses and Aaron called the community together at the rock. Moses shouted, “Listen, you rebels! Must we get water out of this rock for you?”
Moses lifted his arm and hit the rock twice with the staff. A great flow of water burst out, and the people drank, as did their livestock.

But Yahweh said to Moses and Aaron, “You failed to rely on me and did not treat me as holy before the Israelites. For this you will not be the ones to lead this community into the land I am giving them.”
These are the waters of Meribah,{b} where the Israelites argued with Yahweh and showed that he is holy.{c}
Moses dispatched envoys from Kadesh to the king of Edom: “This is what your brother Israel says. You are aware of every hardship that has fallen on us.
Our forefathers went down into Egypt and stayed for years. The Egyptians abused both us and our forefathers.
We cried to Yahweh, and he listened. He sent an angel,{d} and he led us out of Egypt. Now here we sit at Kadesh, a town right on the border of your territory.

Please allow us to pass through your country. We will not walk through fields or vineyards, and we will not drink well water. We will stay on the King’s Highway{e} and will not turn right or left until we are past your borders.”
Edom replied, “You will not cross our land. If you try, we will come out with swords to meet you.”
The Israelites answered, “We will keep to the highway. If any of our animals drink your water, we will pay the price. All we ask is to travel on foot, nothing more.”
Edom replied, “You may not pass.” Then Edom marched out against them with a huge, powerful army.
Since Edom would not let Israel through its land, Israel turned away.
The entire Israelite community set out from Kadesh and reached Mount Hor.
At Mount Hor, near the border of Edom, Yahweh said to Moses and Aaron,
“Aaron is about to be gathered to his ancestors. He will never enter the land I am giving the Israelites, because both of you disobeyed my command at the waters of Meribah.
Bring Aaron and his son Eleazar to the top of Mount Hor.
Strip Aaron of his priestly garments and dress Eleazar in them. Aaron will be gathered to his ancestors and die on the mountain.”
Moses obeyed Yahweh. With the entire community watching, the three of them climbed Mount Hor.
There Moses removed Aaron’s garments and dressed his son Eleazar in them. Aaron died on the mountaintop. Then Moses and Eleazar descended.
The whole community saw that Aaron was dead, and all the people of Israel wept for him for thirty days.{f}

notes.text: The first month, Abib (later Nisan). Its dates fall in different parts of March and April from year to year, because the months followed the moon. The year is not stated; it is usually taken to be the fortieth year after leaving Egypt (compare 33:38).
Meribah means “arguing.” Compare Exodus 17:7.

The Hebrew verb for “showed that he is holy” (yiqqadesh) echoes the name Kadesh. At this point the Samaritan Pentateuch adds material from Deuteronomy 3:24-28, in which Moses begs to enter the land. A Dead Sea Scroll, 4QNum-b, has a similar addition. See the note at 10:10.
Or “a messenger.”
The ancient main road east of the Jordan River, running from Damascus south to the Gulf of Aqaba.
According to 33:38, Aaron died on the first day of the fifth month (July-August) of the fortieth year.

verses.text: The Canaanite king of Arad, who lived in the Negev, learned that Israel was coming along the Atharim road.{a} He attacked Israel and captured some of the people.
Then Israel vowed to Yahweh: “Hand this people over to us, and we will wipe out their cities for you.”{b}
Yahweh heard Israel’s plea and gave the Canaanites to them. Israel devoted them and their cities to destruction, and the spot was named Hormah.{c}
The people left Mount Hor on the road to the Red Sea,{d} to circle around the land of Edom. Along the way they lost heart.
They turned on God and on Moses, saying, “Was it your idea to drag us from Egypt so we could perish in this wasteland? There’s no bread and no water, and we are sick of this wretched food!”
So Yahweh let loose poisonous snakes{e} against them. Their bites killed many in Israel.
The survivors came to Moses and confessed, “We were wrong to speak against Yahweh and you. Pray that Yahweh removes these snakes.” Moses interceded for the people.
Yahweh instructed Moses, “Make a burning snake and put it up on a pole. Every bitten person who looks at it will survive.”
Moses shaped a snake out of bronze{f} and fastened it to a pole. From then on, whenever a snake bit someone, he looked at the bronze snake and lived.
Israel broke camp and settled next at Oboth.
After leaving Oboth they camped at Iye-abarim,{g} in the desert that faces Moab on the east.
Leaving there, they set up camp in the Zered Valley.
Moving from that spot, they camped across the Arnon, in the desert that stretches out from the Amorite border. The Arnon marks Moab’s edge, with Moab on one side and the Amorites on the other.
This is why the Book of the Wars of Yahweh{h} speaks of “Waheb in Suphah{i} and the ravines of the Arnon,
the slopes of those ravines that run down toward the town of Ar and lean against Moab’s border.”
From there they traveled to Beer.{j} This is the well where Yahweh told Moses, “Call the people together, and I will give them water.”
It was then that Israel sang: “Well, spring up! Sing about it!
This is the well that princes dug, that the nobles of the nation scooped out with royal scepters and their own staffs.” After the desert they came to Mattanah,{k}
and after Mattanah to Nahaliel, then to Bamoth.
Beyond Bamoth lies the valley in Moab’s land, below the top of Pisgah, which overlooks the wasteland.{l}
Israel sent envoys to Sihon, the Amorite king, with this request:
“Let us go through your country. We will not leave the road for any field or vineyard, and we will drink no well water. We will stay on the King’s Highway until we are past your border.”
Sihon would not allow Israel through. Instead he called out his whole army, marched into the desert to meet Israel, and attacked them at Jahaz.
Israel killed him with the sword and took his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok, up to the Ammonite border, which was fortified.{m}
Israel took all these towns and lived in the Amorite towns, including Heshbon and the villages around it.{n}
Heshbon had been the capital of Sihon, the Amorite king. He had earlier fought the king of Moab and taken all his land as far as the Arnon.
That is why the poets say: “Come to Heshbon! Let it be rebuilt, and let Sihon’s city stand firm.
A fire spread from Heshbon, flames out of Sihon’s city. It burned up Ar in Moab and the rulers of the Arnon’s heights.{o}
You are doomed, Moab! You are finished, people of Chemosh!{p} He turned his sons into refugees and his daughters into captives of Sihon, the Amorite king.
We shot them down. Heshbon is ruined all the way to Dibon. We left it in waste as far as Nophah, near Medeba.”{q}
So Israel made their home in the Amorites’ land.
Moses sent spies to scout Jazer. Israel took its villages and drove out the Amorites living there.
Turning north, they climbed the road toward Bashan. Og, Bashan’s king, brought out his entire army to meet them in battle at Edrei.
Yahweh told Moses, “Do not fear him. I have handed him over to you, with his army and land. Treat him the way you treated Sihon, the Amorite king who ruled in Heshbon.”
Israel killed him, his sons, and all his people, until no one was left, and they took over his land.

notes.text: Or “the way of the spies.” The meaning of Atharim is uncertain.
Hebrew kharam, to give something to God permanently, usually by destroying it.
Hormah means “destruction.”
Hebrew yam suf, “Sea of Reeds.” Here it probably means the Gulf of Aqaba. See the note at Exodus 10:19.
Hebrew seraf, “burning one,” probably for the burning pain of the bite. The same word is used of the winged beings in Isaiah 6:2.
Hebrew nekhash nekhoshet, a wordplay: “a serpent of bronze.” King Hezekiah later smashed it because people had begun to worship it (2 Kings 18:4). Compare John 3:14-15.

Iye-abarim means “ruins of Abarim” or “ruins of the regions beyond.” At several points in this chapter (after verses 11, 12, 20, and 21) the Samaritan Pentateuch adds material drawn from Deuteronomy 2. See the note at 10:10.
A lost collection of poems about Israel’s battles, known only from this quotation.
The Hebrew is uncertain. Waheb and Suphah may be place names, and the line has no verb because the quotation begins in the middle of a sentence.
Beer means “well.”
Mattanah means “gift.” Nahaliel means “valley of God.” Bamoth means “heights.”
Or “Jeshimon.”
The Greek Old Testament reads “for Jazer was the Ammonite border.”
Hebrew “daughters.”
Or “the high places of the Arnon.”
Chemosh was the national god of Moab.

The meaning of verse 30 is uncertain. The Greek Old Testament reads “fire” (Hebrew ‘esh) where the Hebrew has “which” (‘asher), a reading many scholars prefer: “and fire was kindled as far as Medeba.”

verses.text: The Israelites traveled on and camped on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan across from Jericho.{a}
Balak son of Zippor{b} had watched everything Israel did to the Amorites.
The size of the Israelite crowd terrified Moab. Moab felt sick with dread.
The Moabites told the elders of Midian, “This crowd is going to eat up everything around us, the way an ox munches field grass.” Balak son of Zippor was king of Moab then.

He sent messengers to Balaam son of Beor{c} at Pethor, near the Euphrates,{d} in the homeland of his relatives.{e} They said, “A people has come up out of Egypt. They cover the land, and they have settled right next to me.

Come to my aid, please, and put a curse on this people. They are too strong for me. If you do, I may be able to defeat them and drive them from this land. I am aware that those you bless are blessed, and those you curse are cursed.”
The elders of Moab and Midian left with the money for a fortune-teller in hand. They reached Balaam and passed on Balak’s message.
Balaam replied, “Spend the night with me. In the morning I will give you whatever answer Yahweh gives.” The Moabite princes lodged there.
God visited Balaam with a question: “Who are the men with you?”
Balaam replied, “King Balak of Moab, son of Zippor, has sent me this word:
‘A people who came out of Egypt now covers the land. Come and curse them for me. Maybe then I can fight them and drive them away.’”
God said, “You are not to go with them. And you must not put a curse on this people, for I have blessed them.”
In the morning Balaam got up and told Balak’s officials, “Go back to your country. Yahweh will not allow me to go with you.”
So the Moabite officials went back to Balak and reported, “Balaam would not come with us.”
Balak sent another group of officials, more of them and higher in rank than the first.
They arrived at Balaam’s and delivered the message: “This is from Balak son of Zippor. I urge you, let nothing hold you back from coming to me.
You will be paid generously, and whatever you request, I will carry out. Only come, and put a curse on this people for me.”
Balaam replied to the officials, “If Balak offered me a house filled with silver and gold, I still could not defy Yahweh my God in any matter, great or small.
Now, you too should stay here overnight, and I will find out what else Yahweh may tell me.”
God came to Balaam that night. “Since these men are here to summon you, go along. But you must do exactly and only what I say.”
So in the morning Balaam saddled his donkey and set off with the Moabite princes.
God was angry that he went, and Yahweh’s angel{f} stood in the road to block{g} him. Balaam was riding his donkey, with two servants beside him.
The donkey saw Yahweh’s angel in the road with a drawn sword in his hand. She turned off the road into a field. Balaam hit her to steer her back to the road.
Next the angel took a position on a path running between vineyards, hemmed in by walls left and right.
When the donkey saw the angel, she pressed against the wall and squeezed Balaam’s foot against it. He hit her again.
The angel went on ahead and stood where the road narrowed and left no space to veer either way.
When the donkey saw the angel, she lay down under Balaam. Balaam lost his temper and beat her with his staff.
Then Yahweh enabled the donkey to speak. “What did I ever do to you,” she said to Balaam, “that you have beaten me three times?”
Balaam shot back, “You have made me look ridiculous! If only I were holding a sword, you would be dead by now.”
The donkey said, “Am I not the donkey you have ridden your whole life, right up to today? Have I ever acted like this before?” “No,” he said.
Then Yahweh uncovered Balaam’s eyes, and he saw the angel in the road, sword out. He knelt and bowed with his face to the ground.
Yahweh’s angel demanded, “Why have you beaten your donkey these three times? I am the one who came to block you, because the road you are on is headed the wrong way.{h}
Your donkey spotted me and shied away three separate times. If she had not, you would be dead now, and she would be alive.”
Balaam said to the angel, “I was wrong. I had no idea you were there in my way. If you object, I will go home.”
The angel replied, “Go along with them. Speak only what I give you to say.” Balaam continued with Balak’s princes.
Hearing Balaam was on his way, Balak met him at Ir-moab,{i} by the Arnon, right at his border.
“Did I not send you an urgent invitation?” Balak asked. “Why did you hold back? Do you think I am unable to pay you well?”
“I have arrived,” Balaam said, “but I have no power to say whatever I like. Only what God puts in my mouth will I say.”
Balaam then went with Balak to Kiriath-huzoth.{j}
Balak sacrificed cattle and sheep, and sent portions to Balaam and the officials with him.
At dawn Balak took Balaam up to Bamoth-baal,{k} where he could look out on the edge of the Israelite camp.

notes.text: Hebrew “beyond the Jordan of Jericho,” that is, east of the Jordan, opposite Jericho.
Balak perhaps means “devastator.” Zippor means “bird.”

Balaam perhaps means “devourer.” Beor means “burning.” A plaster wall inscription from about 800 BC, found at Deir ‘Alla in Jordan, tells of a seer named “Balaam son of Beor” who received a vision from the gods at night.
Hebrew “the River,” the Euphrates.
Or “in the land of the Amawites,” a people known from ancient inscriptions. The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Syriac, and the Latin Vulgate read “the land of the Ammonites.”
Or “Yahweh’s messenger,” a heavenly being who speaks and acts for Yahweh, at times as Yahweh himself. So throughout this chapter. Compare Exodus 3:2.
Hebrew satan, “adversary” or “opponent.” So also in verse 32.
The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain; perhaps “perverse” or “headlong.”
Or “the city of Moab.”
Kiriath-huzoth means “city of streets.”
Bamoth-baal means “high places of Baal.”

verses.text: Balaam told Balak, “Build seven altars for me here, and get seven bulls and seven rams ready.”
Balak did just that. A bull and a ram went on each altar, offered by Balak and Balaam together.
Balaam told Balak, “Stay beside your burnt offering. I am going off alone; maybe Yahweh will meet me. Whatever he reveals, I will report to you.” Then he climbed a bare hilltop.{a}
God met Balaam, who said, “I have set up seven altars, and offered a bull and a ram on every one.”
Yahweh put words into Balaam’s mouth and told him, “Return to Balak. Here is what you must tell him.”
Balaam returned. Balak and every Moabite leader were still standing next to his burnt offering.
Balaam gave this poem:{b} “Balak fetched me from Aram, the king of Moab from the eastern ridges. ‘Curse Jacob for me,’ he said. ‘Come, shout down Israel!’
How can I curse people God has not cursed? How can I shout against people Yahweh has not condemned?
From the rocky heights I see them. From the hills I look down on them. Here is a nation living apart, not counting itself among the other nations.
Who can tally the dust-like crowds of Jacob, or count even one quarter{c} of Israel? Let my death be the death of the upright, and let my last days resemble theirs!”
“What is this you have done?” Balak said to Balaam. “My enemies were the ones I wanted cursed, and all you have given them is blessing!”
Balaam answered, “Do I not have to speak exactly what Yahweh puts in my mouth?”
Balak urged him, “Come with me to a different spot. From there you will view just a portion of them, not the whole camp. Put your curse on them from that place.”
He led Balaam to the Lookouts’ Field{d} on Pisgah’s summit. On it he erected seven altars and laid a bull and a ram on each.
Balaam said to Balak, “Wait here by your burnt offering while I meet Yahweh over there.”
Yahweh met Balaam, gave him a message, and said, “Return to Balak. Here is what you must tell him.”
Balaam came back. Balak was beside his burnt offering with Moab’s leaders. “What has Yahweh declared?” Balak wanted to know.
Then Balaam spoke his poem: “Stand up, Balak, and hear this. Listen to me, son of Zippor.
God is no mere man, who could lie. He is no human being, who might change his mind. When he speaks, does he fail to act? When he promises, does he fail to deliver?
I was told to bless. He has blessed, and I cannot take it back.
No disaster is seen in Jacob, and no trouble is found in Israel.{e} Yahweh their God is with them. They shout for joy because their king is among them.
God is leading them out of Egypt with the strength of a wild ox.{f}
No sorcery works against Jacob, and no omen reads against Israel.{g} The day is coming when people will say of Jacob and Israel, ‘Look at the deeds of God!’
This nation rises like a lioness and stands like a lion. It will not rest until it has eaten its catch and drunk the blood of the slain.”
Balak said to Balaam, “If you will not curse them, then do not bless them either!”
Balaam answered, “Did I not tell you that I must do everything Yahweh says?”
Balak went on, “Let me bring you to another place. It may be that God will agree to your cursing them for me there.”
Balak then brought Balaam to the peak of Peor, which looks out over the wasteland.
Balaam told Balak, “Build seven altars for me here, and get seven bulls and seven rams ready.”
Balak did what Balaam said and offered a bull and a ram on every altar.

notes.text: The Hebrew word shefi is uncertain. It may mean a bare hill, or “alone.”
Hebrew mashal, a word used for proverbs, parables, taunts, and spoken oracles. So also in verse 18 and in chapter 24.
Or “the dust clouds.” The Hebrew word rova’ is uncertain. The Greek Old Testament reads “the families,” and some other ancient versions read “the multitudes.”
Zophim means “watchers” or “lookouts.”
Or “No one has seen wrongdoing in Jacob, or trouble in Israel.”
Or “the strength of a wild ox.” The meaning of the Hebrew to’afot is uncertain.
Or “in Jacob ... in Israel,” meaning that Israel does not practice fortune-telling.

verses.text: Balaam now understood that Yahweh was pleased to bless Israel. He did not go off to hunt for omens as before, but turned toward the desert.
When Balaam looked up, he saw Israel camped tribe by tribe, and God’s Spirit came on him.
He gave this poem: “Here is what Balaam son of Beor declares, what the man with open eyes declares,{a}
the message of one who hears what God says and sees what the Almighty{b} shows him, who falls down with his eyes wide open:
How lovely are your tents, Jacob, and your homes, Israel!
They spread out like valleys, like gardens by a river, like aloe trees planted by Yahweh, like cedars beside the water.
Water will pour from their buckets, and their seed will have plenty of water.{c} Their king will rise above Agag,{d} and their kingdom will be lifted high.
God leads them out of Egypt, as strong as a wild ox. They will devour hostile nations, shatter their bones, and pierce them with arrows.
Israel crouches, then stretches out like a lion, a lioness. Who dares to disturb him? A blessing on everyone who blesses you, and a curse on everyone who curses you.”
Balak was seething. He slapped his hands together and told Balaam, “I summoned you to curse my enemies, and three times in a row you have blessed them.
Get out of here and go home! I promised you great honor, but Yahweh has kept it from you.”
Balaam said to Balak, “Did I not tell the very messengers you sent to me
‘If Balak handed over a house packed with silver and gold, I would still be unable to break Yahweh’s command, whether for good or evil by my own choice. What Yahweh says is what I will say’?
Now I am going back to my people. But first let me tell you what this people will do to your people in the days ahead.”
He gave this poem: “Here is what Balaam son of Beor declares, what the man with open eyes declares,
the message of one who hears what God says, who has knowledge from the Most High,{e} and sees what the Almighty shows him, who falls down with his eyes wide open:

I see someone, though not now. I behold him, though he is not near. A star will step out from Jacob, and a scepter{f} will rise from Israel. He will strike Moab on the forehead{g} and tear down all the sons of Sheth.{h}
Edom will be taken over. Seir, its enemy, will be taken over too, while Israel grows strong.
A ruler will come from Jacob and wipe out whoever survives in the city.”
Balaam looked toward Amalek and spoke his poem: “Amalek was the first among nations, but it will come to ruin in the end.”
Then he looked toward the Kenites and spoke his poem: “Your home is safe, and your nest sits high in the rocks.{i}
Yet Kain will be destroyed when Asshur takes you captive.”{j}
Then he spoke once more: “Who can live when God brings this about?{k}
Ships will sail in from Kittim’s coast{l} to humble Asshur and Eber. In the end Kittim too will perish.”
With that, Balaam rose and returned to his own place. Balak went off as well.

notes.text: Or “closed.” The meaning of the Hebrew shetum is uncertain. So also in verse 15.
Hebrew Shaddai, a name for God of uncertain meaning, often translated “the Almighty.” So also in verse 16.
The meaning of this line is uncertain. The Greek Old Testament reads, “A man will come out of his seed, and he will rule many nations.”
Agag was a king of the Amalekites (compare 1 Samuel 15:8). The Greek Old Testament and some other ancient sources read “Gog.”
Hebrew ‘Elyon.

Hebrew shevet, “scepter” or “tribe.” The Greek Old Testament reads “a man.” Later Jewish and Christian readers took this verse as a promise of a coming king. The Dead Sea Scrolls quote it (for example in the Damascus Document and 4QTestimonia), and the second-century leader Simeon bar Kosiba was called Bar Kokhba, “son of the star.”
Or “the borders.” Hebrew “the two sides of the head.”
Or “the sons of tumult.” Compare Jeremiah 48:45. Sheth may be the name of a people.
The Hebrew word qen, “nest,” plays on Qayin, “Kain,” the ancestor of the Kenites in verse 22.
The meaning of verses 21-22 is uncertain. Asshur is Assyria, or possibly a tribe of that name (Genesis 25:3).

The Hebrew of verses 23-24 is very hard to read. The Greek Old Testament begins this saying with “And he looked at Og.” Some scholars change the Hebrew to read “Who will live among the islands of the north?”
Kittim is Cyprus, and by extension the peoples along the western Mediterranean coasts.

verses.text: Israel was staying at Shittim{a} when the men started having affairs with Moabite women.
The women asked them to attend feasts held for their gods. The Israelites ate there and bowed down to those gods.
So Israel joined in worshiping Baal of Peor,{b} and Yahweh grew angry with them.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Seize every chief of the people and hang them{c} before Yahweh in open sunlight, so that Yahweh’s fierce anger will leave Israel.”
Moses gave this order to Israel’s judges: “Every one of you is to kill whichever of your men have joined in the worship of Baal of Peor.”
Just then, as Moses and the entire community stood weeping at the doorway of the meeting tent, an Israelite brought a Midianite woman home to his relatives, right in front of them.
Phinehas{d} saw it. He was the son of Eleazar, who was Aaron the priest’s son. He left the assembly and took up a spear.
He went after the man into the tent{e} and drove the spear through the two of them, through the man and into the woman’s stomach. That stopped the plague among the Israelites.
The plague had killed 24,000 people.
Yahweh spoke to Moses:
“Phinehas, Eleazar’s son and the grandson of Aaron the priest, has calmed my wrath toward the Israelites. His devotion to my honor matched my own, so I held back from wiping them out in my anger.
Announce to him that I am granting him my covenant of peace.
The priesthood will be his for good, and his descendants’ after him, because he burned with zeal for his God and made things right for the Israelites.”
The Israelite who was struck down along with the Midianite woman was Zimri, Salu’s son, the head of a Simeonite family.
The slain Midianite woman was Cozbi, whose father Zur ruled over a clan of Midianite families.{f}
Yahweh instructed Moses,
“Make the Midianites your enemies and attack them,
They treated you as enemies first, tricking you in the matter of Peor and of Cozbi, the daughter of a Midianite leader and their countrywoman, who was killed on the day of the plague at Peor.”{g}

notes.text: Shittim means “acacia trees.”
Baal means “lord” or “master,” a title of a Canaanite storm god. Baal of Peor was the god worshiped at Peor (compare 23:28).
The meaning of the Hebrew verb is uncertain. It may mean to impale, to hang, or to expose the bodies after breaking the limbs. The Greek Old Testament reads “make an example of them.”
Phinehas is an Egyptian name meaning “the Nubian.”
The Hebrew word qubbah, found only here, probably means a tent shrine or inner room.
Zimri means “my protection” or “my song.” Salu’s meaning is uncertain. Cozbi perhaps means “deceitful” or “voluptuous.” Zur means “rock.”
In the Hebrew text, the next sentence, “After the plague,” is verse 19 of chapter 25. In English Bibles it begins 26:1.

verses.text: After the plague, Yahweh said to Moses and to Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest,
“Take a count of the whole Israelite community, listing by family everyone twenty or older who can serve in the army.”
So Moses and Eleazar the priest gave this order on the plains of Moab by the Jordan, across from Jericho:
“Count the people from age twenty up,” as Yahweh had told Moses.{a} The Israelites who had come out of Egypt were these:
Reuben was Israel’s oldest son. His sons were Hanoch, who founded the Hanochite clan, and Pallu, who founded the Palluite clan,
and Hezron, founder of the Hezronites, and Carmi, founder of the Carmites.
The Reubenite clans totaled 43,730 men.
Pallu fathered Eliab.
Nemuel, Dathan, and Abiram were Eliab’s three sons. Dathan and Abiram were the ones chosen by the community who opposed Moses and Aaron as part of Korah’s group when it opposed Yahweh.
The earth opened its mouth and swallowed them along with Korah, when that group perished, and fire consumed 250 men. These became a lesson to all.
Korah’s sons, however, did not die.
Simeon’s clans: Nemuel gave his name to the Nemuelites, Jamin to the Jaminites, and Jachin to the Jachinites,
Zerah to the Zerahites, and Shaul to the Shaulites.
The Simeonite clans totaled 22,200 men.
Gad’s clans: Zephon led to the Zephonites, Haggi to the Haggites, and Shuni to the Shunites,
Ozni to the Oznites, and Eri to the Erites,
Arod to the Arodites, and Areli to the Arelites.
The Gadite clans came to 40,500 men in all.
Judah’s first two sons, Er and Onan, died while still in Canaan.
The other clans of Judah came from Shelah (the Shelanites), Perez (the Perezites), and Zerah (the Zerahites).
Perez had two sons who also founded clans: Hezron (the Hezronites) and Hamul (the Hamulites).
Judah’s clans totaled 76,500 men.
Issachar’s clans came from Tola (the Tolaites) and Puvah (the Punites),
Jashub (the Jashubites) and Shimron (the Shimronites).
The clans of Issachar totaled 64,300 men.
Zebulun’s clans came from Sered (the Seredites), Elon (the Elonites), and Jahleel (the Jahleelites).
The Zebulunite clans totaled 60,500 men.
Joseph’s descendants formed two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim.
Manasseh’s line began with Machir, whose son Gilead gave his name to the Gileadite clan; Machir’s family were the Machirites.
Gilead’s clans came from Iezer{b} (the Iezerites) and Helek (the Helekites),
Asriel (the Asrielites) and Shechem (the Shechemites),
Shemida (the Shemidaites) and Hepher (the Hepherites).
Zelophehad, Hepher’s son, had no male children, just daughters. They were Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.{c}
Manasseh’s clans totaled 52,700 men.
Ephraim’s clans came from Shuthelah (the Shuthelahites), Becher (the Becherites), and Tahan (the Tahanites).
Shuthelah’s son Eran began the Eranite clan.
Ephraim’s clans totaled 32,500 men. All of these were Joseph’s descendants, listed by clan.
Benjamin’s clans came from Bela (the Belaites), Ashbel (the Ashbelites), and Ahiram (the Ahiramites),
Shephupham{d} (the Shuphamites) and Hupham (the Huphamites).
Bela had two sons, Ard and Naaman, who started the Ardite and Naamite clans.
Benjamin’s clans totaled 45,600 men.
Dan’s only clan came from Shuham, so the Shuhamites were the one family of Dan.
That clan alone numbered 64,400 men.
Asher’s clans came from Imnah (the Imnites), Ishvi (the Ishvites), and Beriah (the Beriites).
Beriah’s sons began two more clans: Heber (the Heberites) and Malchiel (the Malchielites).
Asher also had a daughter named Serah.
Asher’s clans totaled 53,400 men.
Naphtali’s clans came from Jahzeel (the Jahzeelites) and Guni (the Gunites),
Jezer (the Jezerites) and Shillem (the Shillemites).
The clans of Naphtali totaled 45,400 men.
The full count of Israelite men came to 601,730.{e}
Yahweh said to Moses,
“Divide the land among these tribes as their inheritance, based on how many names are on the lists.
Give a bigger share to a big tribe and a smaller share to a small tribe. Each gets land in proportion to its count.
The land is to be divided by drawing lots, and each tribe will inherit by the names of its ancestral tribes.
Lots will decide each share, whether the tribe is large or small.”
The Levite clans were counted too. They came from Gershon (the Gershonites), Kohath (the Kohathites), and Merari (the Merarites).
More Levite families were Libni’s, Hebron’s, Mahli’s, Mushi’s, and Korah’s. Kohath fathered Amram.
Amram married Jochebed, a daughter of Levi who had been born in Egypt. Together they had Aaron, Moses, and their sister Miriam.
Aaron’s sons were Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
Nadab and Abihu died after they brought forbidden fire before Yahweh.
The Levites numbered 23,000, every male a month old or more. They were left out of the general count because no land was set aside for them among the Israelites.
These were the people Moses and Eleazar the priest registered on the plains of Moab, near the Jordan opposite Jericho.
Not one of them had been counted in the earlier census by Moses and Aaron the priest in the Sinai Desert.
Yahweh had said of that generation, “They will die in the desert.” Not one was left except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun.

notes.text: The words “Count the people” are not in the Hebrew, which is abrupt here. They are supplied from verse 2.
In Joshua 17:2 the name is Abiezer.
Mahlah perhaps means “weakness.” Noah (a different name from Noah of the flood) means “movement.” Hoglah means “partridge,” Milcah “queen,” and Tirzah “pleasing.”
The traditional Hebrew text. Some manuscripts and ancient versions read “Shupham,” matching the clan name, and Genesis 46:21 has Muppim.
The total is slightly less than the 603,550 of the first census (1:46). On what the numbers mean, see the note at 1:46.

verses.text: Then Zelophehad’s daughters stepped up. Their father was a son of Hepher, a descendant of Gilead, Machir, and Manasseh, who was Joseph’s son. The sisters were Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.
They took their place in front of Moses, Eleazar the priest, the chiefs, and all the people gathered at the doorway of the meeting tent, and said,
“Our father perished in the wilderness. He did not side with Korah’s mob against Yahweh. His own sin cost him his life, and he had no sons.
Must his name fade out of his clan only because he had no son? We ask you to give us a property holding among our father’s kin.”
Moses took their case to Yahweh.{a}
Yahweh told Moses,
“Zelophehad’s daughters are correct. Without fail, give them a holding of land among their father’s kin, and hand their father’s share over to them.
Say to the Israelites: If a man dies with no son, his inheritance goes to his daughter.
With no daughter, it goes to his brothers.
With no brothers, his father’s brothers receive it.
If his father had no brothers either, give it to the closest relative in his clan, who will own it. This will be a legal rule for the Israelites, just as Yahweh commanded Moses.”
Yahweh said to Moses, “Go up this peak in the Abarim range{b} and view the country I am giving the Israelites.
After one look at it, you will die and be laid with your relatives, as Aaron your brother was.
In the Zin Desert, when the community fought with me, both of you defied my command to honor me as holy in front of them at the water.” (This is the water of Meribah at Kadesh in the Zin Desert.)
Moses said to Yahweh,
“Yahweh, God who gives breath to every living thing, please choose a man to lead this community.
He will lead them out to battle and bring them home again, so that Yahweh’s people will not be like a flock with no shepherd.”
Yahweh told Moses, “Pick Joshua, the son of Nun, who is a man filled with the Spirit,{c} and rest your hand on him.
Bring him up before Eleazar the priest and everyone gathered, and give him his charge as they look on.
Place a portion of your own authority on him, so the whole Israelite community will follow him.

He will stand before Eleazar the priest, who will learn my decisions for him by using the Urim{d} before Yahweh. At Joshua’s word they will go out, and at his word they will come in, he and the whole community of Israel.”
Moses did what Yahweh commanded. He set Joshua before Eleazar the priest and the entire assembly,
laid his hands on him, and gave him his task, as Yahweh had said through Moses.{e}

notes.text: In the traditional Hebrew text, the last letter of the word for “their case” (mishpatan) is written larger than normal.
Abarim means “regions beyond.” It is the mountain range east of the Dead Sea that includes Mount Nebo (Deuteronomy 32:49).
Or “spirit.”
The Urim and Thummim were objects kept in the high priest’s chest piece and used to learn God’s will (Exodus 28:30). Their meaning is uncertain. Urim may be related to ‘or, “light.”
At this point the Samaritan Pentateuch adds material from Deuteronomy 3:21-22, where Moses encourages Joshua. A Dead Sea Scroll, 4QNum-b, has a similar addition. See the note at 10:10.

subheads.12: Moses will see the land but not enter

verses.text: Yahweh told Moses,
“Give the Israelites this order: Be careful to bring me my offering at the right time. It is my food, a gift made by fire that makes a smell pleasing to me.
Tell them: This is the gift made by fire that you are to bring Yahweh: two male lambs, each a year old with no flaw, every day, as a standing burnt offering.
Offer one lamb in the morning and the second at dusk,{a}
along with about 2 quarts of fine flour as a grain offering, mixed with about 1 quart of oil from crushed olives.{b}
This is the standing burnt offering started at Mount Sinai, a smell that pleases Yahweh, a gift made by fire.
Include a drink offering of about 1 quart for each lamb. At the holy place, pour out strong drink{c} to Yahweh as the drink offering.
The second lamb goes up at dusk. Along with it, bring the same grain offering and drink offering as in the morning. It is a gift made by fire, a smell that pleases Yahweh.
“On the Sabbath, bring two male lambs, each a year old with no flaw, with a grain offering of about 4 quarts of fine flour{d} mixed with oil, and the drink offering.
This is the Sabbath burnt offering. It is added to the standing burnt offering and its drink offering.
“At the start of each month,{e} bring Yahweh a burnt offering of two young bulls, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old with no flaw.
For each bull, add a grain offering of about 6 quarts of fine flour mixed with oil. For the ram, add about 4 quarts of fine flour mixed with oil.
For each lamb, add a grain offering of about 2 quarts of fine flour mixed with oil.{f} This is a burnt offering, a gift made by fire with a smell that pleases Yahweh.
The drink offerings are about 2 quarts of wine for each bull, about 1⅓ quarts for the ram, and about 1 quart for each lamb.{g} This is the offering for the first day of every month, all year long.
Also offer one male goat to Yahweh as a sin offering. It is added to the standing burnt offering and its drink offering.
“The fourteenth day of the first month (March-April){h} is Yahweh’s Passover.
The festival starts on the fifteenth of that month, and for a full week the bread you eat is made without yeast.
Hold a holy gathering on the first of those days, and do no ordinary work.
Bring Yahweh a gift made by fire, a burnt offering of two young bulls, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old. All of them must be flawless.
With them bring grain offerings of fine flour mixed with oil: about 6 quarts for each bull and about 4 quarts for the ram.
For each of the seven lambs, bring about 2 quarts.
Add one male goat as a sin offering, to make things right for you.
Offer all of these in addition to the morning burnt offering that is part of the standing offering.
Do the same each day for seven days, as food for the gift made by fire, a smell that pleases Yahweh. It is offered in addition to the standing burnt offering and its drink offering.
The seventh day brings another holy gathering. Do no ordinary work.
“On the day of firstfruits,{i} when you bring Yahweh a new grain offering at your Festival of Weeks, hold a holy gathering. Do no ordinary work.
Bring a burnt offering with a smell that pleases Yahweh: two young bulls, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old.
For each bull, the grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil is about 6 quarts; for the ram, about 4 quarts;
and about 2 quarts for each of the seven lambs.
Add one male goat, to make things right for you.
Offer these in addition to the standing burnt offering with its grain offering, along with their drink offerings. Make sure the animals have no flaw.”

notes.text: Hebrew “between the two evenings,” probably the time between sunset and dark. So also in verse 8. See the note at Exodus 12:6.

Hebrew “a tenth of an ephah of fine flour ... a quarter of a hin of beaten oil,” about 2.2 liters of flour and 0.9 liter of oil. An ephah was about three-fifths of a bushel (22 liters), and a hin about 1 gallon (3.7 liters). Standards varied. So also with the drink offering in verse 7.
Hebrew shekar, a fermented drink, possibly beer.
Hebrew “two-tenths,” about 4.4 liters.
Hebrew “heads of your months,” the new moon at the beginning of each lunar month.
Hebrew “three-tenths ... two-tenths ... a tenth” of an ephah, about 6.6, 4.4, and 2.2 liters. The same amounts appear in verses 20-21 and 28-29, and in chapter 29.
Hebrew “half a hin ... a third of a hin ... a quarter of a hin,” about 1.9, 1.2, and 0.9 liters.
The first month, Abib, later called Nisan. Because the months followed the moon, the dates fall in different parts of March and April from year to year.
The Festival of Weeks (Shavuot) came fifty days after the offering of the first sheaf (Leviticus 23:15-16), in the third month, Sivan (May-June).

subheads.16: Passover and the Festival of Unleavened Bread

verses.text: “On the first day of the seventh month (September-October),{a} hold a holy gathering and do no ordinary work. It is a day for blowing trumpets.{b}
Offer a burnt offering with a smell that pleases Yahweh: one young bull, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old, with no flaw.
The grain offering that goes with them is fine flour mixed with oil: about 6 quarts for the bull, about 4 quarts for the ram,
and about 2 quarts for each of the seven lambs.
Bring one male goat as a sin offering, to make things right for you.

Offer all this besides the new-moon offering and its grain, besides the daily burnt offering and its grain, and besides the drinks that go with each. They follow the rules set for them, and they are a smell that pleases Yahweh, a gift made by fire.
“On the tenth day of this seventh month (September-October),{c} hold a holy gathering. You are to deny yourselves{d} and do no work at all.
Bring Yahweh a burnt offering with a smell that pleases him: one young bull, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old. Make sure they are flawless.
The grain that goes with them is fine flour mixed with oil: about 6 quarts for the bull, about 4 quarts for the ram,
and about 2 quarts for each of the seven lambs.

Bring a male goat for a sin offering, too. It is separate from the sin offering used to make things right for the people, and separate from the daily burnt offering, its grain, and the drinks that go with them.
On the fifteenth of the seventh month (September-October),{e} hold a holy gathering and do no ordinary work. For seven days keep a festival for Yahweh.
Bring a burnt offering, a gift made by fire with a smell that pleases Yahweh: thirteen young bulls, two rams, and fourteen male lambs a year old, all without flaw.
For the grain offerings, use fine flour mixed with oil: about 6 quarts for each of the thirteen bulls, about 4 quarts for each of the two rams,
and about 2 quarts for each of the fourteen lambs.
Offer a male goat as a sin offering, too, separate from the daily burnt offering with its grain and its drink.
On the second day, bring twelve young bulls, two rams, and fourteen male lambs a year old, all without a flaw.
Add the grain offerings and drink offerings that go with the bulls, rams, and lambs, as the rule says for their number.
Offer one male goat as a sin offering too, apart from the standing burnt offering with its grain offering and drink offering.{f}
The third day calls for eleven young bulls, two rams, and fourteen flawless male lambs a year old.
Each kind of animal has its own grain offering and drink offering, set by the rule for how many there are.
One male goat is a sin offering as well, apart from the daily burnt offering, its grain offering, and its drink offering.
Offer ten young bulls on the fourth day, together with two rams and fourteen male lambs a year old, none of them flawed.
Bring the grain and the drink offerings for the bulls, rams, and lambs. The amounts match their numbers, as the rule says.
A male goat is also needed as a sin offering. It does not replace the standing burnt offering, its grain offering, or its drink offering.
For the fifth day, prepare nine young bulls, two rams, and fourteen male lambs, each a year old and without defect.
Along with them go the proper grain offerings and drink offerings for bulls, rams, and lambs, counted out by the rule.
One male goat serves as a sin offering as well. This comes on top of the standing burnt offering, its grain offering, and its drink offering.
Day 6 brings eight young bulls, two rams, and fourteen year-old male lambs with no flaw.
The bulls, rams, and lambs each come with their grain offering and drink offering, measured by the number of animals.
Also sacrifice a male goat as a sin offering, over and above the standing burnt offering with its grain and drink offerings.
On day 7, present seven young bulls, two rams, and fourteen male lambs a year old, all perfect.
Supply the grain offering and drink offering for the bulls, rams, and lambs, matching their numbers under the rule.
Provide one male goat for a sin offering, which is added to the standing burnt offering and the grain and drink offerings that go with it.
“On the eighth day, hold a closing assembly.{g} Do no ordinary work.
Bring a burnt offering, a gift made by fire with a smell that pleases Yahweh: one bull, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old, without flaw.
Bring the grain offering and drink offerings that go with the bull, the ram, and the lambs, in amounts matching their numbers, by the rule.
Add one male goat as a sin offering, besides the standing burnt offering, its grain offering, and its drink offering.
“Offer these to Yahweh at your appointed festivals, in addition to your offerings for vows and your freewill offerings, whether burnt offerings, grain offerings, drink offerings, or peace offerings.”
Moses told the Israelites everything Yahweh had ordered him.{h}

notes.text: The seventh month, Tishri, also called Ethanim (1 Kings 8:2). Because the months followed the moon, the dates fall in different parts of September and October from year to year. In later Jewish tradition this day became Rosh Hashanah, the civil New Year.
Hebrew teru’ah, a day of loud blasts, probably on the ram’s horn. Compare Leviticus 23:24.
The Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur). See Leviticus 16:29-34 and 23:26-32.
Or “afflict yourselves,” understood as fasting.
The Festival of Booths (Sukkot). See Leviticus 23:33-43.

In verses 19, 31, and 33 the Hebrew has small irregularities of spelling (“their drink offerings,” “its drink offerings,” “by their rule”). Ancient rabbis noticed that the extra letters spell mayim, “water,” and took this as a hint of the water pouring at the Festival of Booths.
Hebrew ‘atseret, a closing assembly.
In the Hebrew text, verse 40 is numbered 30:1.

verses.text: Moses addressed the heads of the Israelite tribes and said, “Here is what Yahweh has commanded.{a}
If a man makes a promise to Yahweh, or takes an oath that puts him under a pledge, he must not go back on his word. He is to do everything he said.
“Now take a girl who is still young and lives under her father’s roof. She makes a vow to Yahweh and binds herself with a pledge.
If her father learns of the promise or pledge and says nothing, then all her promises stand, and every pledge she took on stands.
But if her father forbids it the day he learns of it, none of her promises or pledges will stand. Yahweh will release her, because her father forbade it.
“Suppose she marries while her promises or a careless word from her lips still bind her.
If her husband hears about it and says nothing that day, her promises stand, and the pledges she took on stand.
But if on the day he hears it her husband refuses to allow it, he cancels the promise she made and the careless word that bound her. Yahweh will release her.
(The promise of a widow or a divorced woman, though, binds her in everything she has pledged.)
“Suppose a woman makes a promise or swears a binding oath while living in her husband’s house.
If her husband hears of it, says nothing, and does not forbid it, all her promises stand, and every pledge she took on stands.
But if he cancels them the same day he hears them, nothing her lips said about those vows or pledges will hold. Her husband voided them, so Yahweh will let her go free.
Her husband may uphold or cancel any promise or binding oath that would have her deny herself.{b}
If he stays quiet toward her day after day, he is confirming all her vows and pledges. By staying quiet when he first heard of them, he has confirmed them.
But if he cancels them some time after he has heard of them, he will carry her guilt.”
These are the rules Yahweh gave Moses about a husband and wife, and about a father and his young daughter living in his house.

notes.text: In the Hebrew text, verses 1-16 are numbered 30:2-17. Verse 1 in Hebrew is what English Bibles number as 29:40.
Or “afflict herself,” probably by fasting.

verses.text: Yahweh said to Moses,
“Take revenge on the Midianites for what they did to Israel. When that is done, you will be gathered to your ancestors.”
So Moses told the people, “Pick men from among you and arm them for war, to attack Midian and carry out Yahweh’s punishment on them.
Send a thousand men from every tribe of Israel into the fight.”
So a thousand were handed over from each tribe, twelve thousand in all, armed for battle.{a}
Moses dispatched them, one thousand per tribe, and sent Phinehas, the son of Eleazar the priest, to go with the army. He took charge of the holy articles and the trumpets used to signal an attack.
They fought Midian just as Yahweh had commanded Moses, and they killed every man.
Five Midianite kings died with the rest: Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba.{b} Balaam son of Beor was also put to the sword.
The Israelite army took the Midianite women and children captive. All the herds, flocks, and goods of Midian they seized as plunder.
They set fire to every town where the Midianites lived and to all their camps.{c}
They gathered up everything they had taken, people and animals alike,
They brought the prisoners and spoils to Moses, to Eleazar the priest, and to the whole Israelite assembly. The camp was on the plains of Moab beside the Jordan, opposite Jericho.
Moses, Eleazar the priest, and every leader of the assembly walked out beyond the camp to greet the army.
Moses was furious with the army’s officers, the commanders over thousands and over hundreds, who were returning from the fighting.
“You let every woman live?” he asked them.
“These are the very women who followed Balaam’s advice and led the Israelites to betray Yahweh at Peor, so that a plague struck Yahweh’s community.
So kill all the boys now, and every woman who has had a man in her bed.
Only the girls who have never had a man in their bed may live, and they are yours.
You must all camp outside for a week. Whoever has taken a life or touched a corpse is to be purified on the third day and the seventh, you and your captives alike.
Purify every garment, and also anything made of leather, goat hair, or wood.”{d}
Next, Eleazar the priest addressed the men who had marched to the battle: “Here is a requirement of the law that Yahweh gave Moses:
Gold, silver, bronze, iron, tin, lead,
whatever survives fire, you must put through fire to make it clean. It must also be cleansed with the purifying water. Whatever cannot survive fire, put through water.
When the seventh day comes, wash your clothes. You will be clean, and then you are free to return to the camp.”
Yahweh told Moses,
“Count all the captured goods, both people and animals. You, Eleazar the priest, and the heads of the clans in the community will do the counting.
Split the loot in two, one share for the soldiers who fought and one for the rest of the community.
From the share belonging to the fighting men, set aside a tax for Yahweh. Take one item in every five hundred, counting people, cattle, donkeys, and sheep or goats alike.
Take it from their half and give it to Eleazar the priest as Yahweh’s portion.

From the other Israelites’ share, take one item in every fifty, whether it is a person, an ox, a donkey, a sheep, a goat, or any other animal. Give these to the Levites, who look after Yahweh’s dwelling.”
Moses and Eleazar the priest did what Yahweh had commanded Moses.
What remained of the plunder the soldiers took came to 675,000 head of sheep and goats,
plus 72,000 cattle,
and 61,000 donkeys,
along with 32,000 women who had never been with a man.
The soldiers’ half came to 337,500 sheep and goats,
of which Yahweh’s tax was 675.
Of the 36,000 cattle, Yahweh’s tax was 72.
Of the 30,500 donkeys, Yahweh’s tax was 61.
Of the 16,000 people, Yahweh’s tax was 32.
Moses gave this tax, which was Yahweh’s portion, to Eleazar the priest, as Yahweh had commanded Moses.
Now for the half that belonged to the rest of the Israelites, which Moses had separated from the soldiers’ half:
The community’s half also held 337,500 sheep and goats,
plus 36,000 cattle,
30,500 donkeys,
and 16,000 people.
Out of the Israelites’ half, Moses chose one in every fifty, people and animals, and gave them to the Levites who looked after Yahweh’s dwelling, as Yahweh had ordered Moses.
Then the commanders of the army’s units of a thousand and a hundred stepped forward to Moses
and said, “We, your servants, have counted the soldiers under our command, and not a single man is missing.
So each of us has brought what gold he could find, as an offering for Yahweh: armbands, bracelets, signet rings, earrings, and necklaces. With it we ask to be made right with Yahweh.”
Moses and Eleazar the priest took the gold ornaments from them, every piece fashioned into jewelry.
All the gold that the commanders of thousands and of hundreds gave Yahweh weighed about 420 pounds.{e}
(The soldiers had kept their own loot.)
Moses and Eleazar the priest brought the officers’ gold to the meeting tent, where it would remind Yahweh of the Israelites.

notes.text: Or “twelve units.” Hebrew ‘elef can mean “thousand” or “clan unit.” See the note at 1:46.
Evi may mean “desire,” Rekem “multicolored,” Zur “rock,” Hur perhaps “white” or “child,” and Reba “fourth” or “offspring.”
Hebrew tirot, walled camps or circular settlements of tents.
At about this point the Samaritan Pentateuch adds more instructions on purification. See the note at 10:10.
Hebrew “16,750 shekels,” about 193 kilograms. A shekel was about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams); standards varied.

verses.text: The tribes of Reuben and Gad owned enormous herds and flocks. Looking over Jazer and Gilead, they saw that the country suited livestock well.
they came to Moses, Eleazar the priest, and the community’s leaders and said,
“Ataroth, Dibon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, Elealeh, Sebam, Nebo, and Beon{a}
are in the country Yahweh conquered for the Israelite community. It is cattle country, and we, your servants, have cattle.”
They went on, “If you are pleased with us, give this land to us as our own. Do not make us cross the Jordan.”
Moses answered the Gadites and Reubenites, “Are your fellow Israelites to go off to war while you stay here?
Why take the heart out of the Israelites, so that they will not cross into the land Yahweh is giving them?
That is just how your fathers acted. I sent them out from Kadesh Barnea to scout the country,
and once they reached the Valley of Eshcol and had seen it, they discouraged the Israelites from going in to the land Yahweh was giving them.
Yahweh’s anger flared up that day, and he made this promise:
‘None of the men who left Egypt, from age twenty up, will see the country I swore to give Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, because they did not follow me wholeheartedly.
Only Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite{b} and Joshua son of Nun are excepted, because they followed Yahweh wholeheartedly.’
Yahweh’s anger blazed against Israel, and he kept them wandering in the desert for forty years, until that entire generation, who had done what was evil in his sight, had died out.
And here you are now, taking your fathers’ place, a crowd of sinners, making Yahweh even angrier at Israel!
If you turn from following him, he will once more leave this people in the desert, and you will bring about their ruin.”
The men stepped closer and said to him, “We want to build pens for our livestock here, and towns for our children.

But we ourselves will arm ourselves and march ahead of the Israelites until we have settled them in their land. In the meantime, our children will stay in walled towns, safe from the people living in this country.
None of us will go home until every Israelite family has its inheritance.
We will not claim any land with them across the Jordan, since our share has come to us here on the east side.”
Moses told them, “If you do this, and go armed to fight in front of Yahweh,
and if every one of your fighting men crosses the Jordan in front of Yahweh until Yahweh has driven out his enemies,
and the land lies conquered before Yahweh, you may then return, with no more duty to Yahweh or Israel, and this land will be yours before Yahweh.
But if you refuse, you will have sinned against Yahweh. Be sure of this: your sin will track you down.
Build towns for your little ones and pens for your sheep if you like, but keep the promise you made.”
The Gadites and Reubenites told Moses, “Your servants will do exactly as my lord orders.
Our wives and little ones, our flocks, and all our herds will stay behind in the towns of Gilead,
while all your servants who are ready for war cross over to fight in front of Yahweh, just as my lord says.”
Then Moses gave instructions concerning these men to Joshua son of Nun, Eleazar the priest, and the clan leaders in each Israelite tribe.
He said, “Suppose the Gadites and Reubenites all cross the Jordan with you, each fit for combat before Yahweh, and the land falls to you. Then Gilead is theirs to keep.
But if they do not cross with you under arms, they must take their land with the rest of you in Canaan.”
The Gadites and Reubenites replied, “We, your servants, will do what Yahweh has said.
We will cross over armed in front of Yahweh into Canaan, and our share of the land will stay with us east of the Jordan.”

Moses gave the half-tribe of Manasseh (descended from Joseph), the Gadites, and the Reubenites the kingdom of Sihon, king of the Amorites, and the kingdom of Og king of Bashan. This was the whole country, its towns, and the lands surrounding each one.
The Gadites rebuilt Dibon, Ataroth, Aroer,
Atroth Shophan, Jazer, Jogbehah,
Beth Nimrah, and Beth Haran as walled towns, and made pens for their sheep.
The Reubenites built up Heshbon, Elealeh, Kiriathaim,
They also rebuilt Nebo, Baal Meon (their names were changed), and Sibmah, and gave other names to the towns they rebuilt.{c}
The descendants of Machir son of Manasseh went to Gilead, conquered it, and drove out the Amorites living there.
Moses gave Gilead to the Machirites, a clan of Manasseh, and they settled there.
Jair, from the tribe of Manasseh, captured some of the villages and named them Havvoth Jair.{d}
Nobah captured Kenath and its surrounding villages and named it Nobah after himself.

notes.text: These are towns east of the Jordan. Sebam is probably Sibmah (verse 38), and Beon is Baal Meon (verse 38).
The Kenizzites were a clan descended from Kenaz, an Edomite (Genesis 36:11), who joined Judah.
Nebo and Baal Meon contain the names of gods (Nabu and Baal), which may explain the renaming.
Havvoth Jair means “tent villages of Jair.”

subheads.1: The tribes east of the Jordan
subheads.33: The land is divided east of the Jordan

verses.text: This is the list of the places where the Israelites stopped after leaving Egypt in their divisions under Moses and Aaron.
At Yahweh’s command, Moses wrote down where they started from and where each stage ended. This is the record of their journey, stage by stage.
They left Rameses on the fifteenth day of the first month (March-April),{a} the day after the Passover. The Israelites marched out boldly{b} while all the Egyptians watched,
Yahweh had struck down their firstborn, and the Egyptians were burying them at that very time. Yahweh also carried out judgments against their gods.
The first camp after Rameses was at Succoth.
Leaving Succoth, they camped at Etham, at the edge of the desert.
Then they swung back in the direction of Pi Hahiroth, which lies to the east of Baal Zephon, and camped in sight of Migdol.
They left Hahiroth{c} and went right through the sea into the desert. After three days’ travel in the Desert of Etham, they camped at Marah.
From Marah they reached Elim, which had twelve springs and seventy palm trees, and they camped there.
They moved on from Elim and camped beside the Red Sea.
They moved on from the Red Sea and camped in the Desert of Sin.
Next they traveled from the Wilderness of Sin to Dophkah, and stayed there.
They set out from Dophkah and stopped at Alush.
From Alush they went to Rephidim, a place with no drinking water for the people.
Rephidim was left behind, and they camped in the Desert of Sinai.
They pulled out of the Desert of Sinai and camped at Kibroth Hattaavah.{d}
After Kibroth Hattaavah came Hazeroth, where they set up camp.
They broke camp at Hazeroth and settled for a time at Rithmah.
Next they traveled from Rithmah to Rimmon Perez, and stayed there.
They set out from Rimmon Perez and stopped at Libnah.
They left Libnah and made camp at Rissah.
From Rissah they moved on to Kehelathah and camped.
Leaving Kehelathah, they pitched their tents at Mount Shepher.
After Mount Shepher came Haradah, where they set up camp.
They broke camp at Haradah and settled for a time at Makheloth.
Next they traveled from Makheloth to Tahath, and stayed there.
They set out from Tahath and stopped at Terah.
They left Terah and made camp at Mithkah.
From Mithkah they moved on to Hashmonah and camped.
Leaving Hashmonah, they pitched their tents at Moseroth.
After Moseroth came Bene Jaakan, where they set up camp.
They broke camp at Bene Jaakan and settled for a time at Hor Haggidgad.
Next they traveled from Hor Haggidgad to Jotbathah, and stayed there.
They set out from Jotbathah and stopped at Abronah.
From Abronah they went on to Ezion Geber and pitched their tents there.
Then they moved into the Desert of Zin, to the place called Kadesh, and camped.
They left Kadesh and pitched camp at Mount Hor, on the border of Edom’s land.
Aaron the priest climbed Mount Hor at Yahweh’s command, and died there on the first day of the fifth month (July-August),{e} forty years after the Israelites had left Egypt.
He was 123 years old at his death on that mountain.
The king of Arad, a Canaanite who ruled in the Negev region of Canaan, got word that the Israelites were approaching.
They set out from Mount Hor and stopped at Zalmonah.
They left Zalmonah and made camp at Punon.
From Punon they moved on to Oboth and camped.
They left Oboth and camped at Iye Abarim, on Moab’s border.
Iyim{f} was their next move, and then they camped at Dibon Gad.
They broke camp at Dibon Gad and settled for a time at Almon Diblathaim.
Next they traveled from Almon Diblathaim to the Abarim mountains, in front of Nebo, and stayed there.
They left the Abarim mountains and camped on the plains of Moab by the Jordan, near Jericho.
Their camp along the Jordan stretched from Beth Jeshimoth to Abel Shittim{g} on the plains of Moab.
Yahweh spoke to Moses on the plains of Moab by the Jordan, near Jericho, and said,
“Tell the Israelites: When you cross the Jordan into Canaan,
drive out everyone living in the land ahead of you. Smash all their carved stones,{h} melt down all their metal idols, and tear down all their places of worship on the hills.
Take possession of the country and settle there, because I have handed it over to you.

You will divide the land among your clans by drawing lots. A large clan gets a large share, and a small clan gets a small one. Each person’s share is wherever the lot falls for him. Your tribal ancestors’ lines decide the shares.

But if you fail to drive out the land’s inhabitants, the ones you let stay will become like splinters in your eyes and thorns in your sides. They will make life hard for you in the land where you live.
In that case, I will do to you what I had planned to do to them.”

notes.text: The first month, Abib, later called Nisan. Because the months followed the moon, the date falls in different parts of March and April from year to year. See Exodus 12:2-6, 51.
Hebrew “with a high hand.”
Some Hebrew manuscripts and ancient versions read “Pi Hahiroth,” as in verse 7.

Verses 16-36 list stopping places, many known only from this passage and impossible to locate today.
